findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity-Above-Limits / Balance Sheet Exposure

For a $5M-$25M revenue PE-backed company, a $5M-$10M uninsured indemnity claim is potentially business-ending.
findings.plain_english: The Maricopa contract specifically says your insurance amount doesn't cap your indemnity owed to the County. Right now your insurance is light or absent on the things most likely to generate big claims. findings.recommendation: This finding is the aggregate of every other missing-policy / underinsurance finding. Cure each underlying gap and the indemnity-uncapped exposure becomes manageable. Independently, build a risk register that maps each contractual indemnity to current insurance capacity vs. balance sheet exposure — quantify the uninsured layer for the PE sponsor and board.

If a $10M indemnity claim landed tomorrow, what's the path — insurance, balance sheet, PE call, all of the above?
When the board last reviewed the insurance program, were they shown the gap between contractual indemnity scope and actual coverage?
Does the PE sponsor's investment agreement actually require certain insurance levels — and if so, are you in compliance?

findings.plain_english: There may be an opportunity at renewal to negotiate a composite rate (one number per $1,000 of revenue) that simplifies audit and stabilizes pricing — worth exploring with carriers at next marketing.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate composite rating at next renewal (4/1/2026). Include in renewal strategy memo to underwriters.

findings.requirement_type: Coverage Across Program — Dependencies on Missing Policies
findings.contract_quote: All applicable contract requirements (Sacramento + Maricopa).

The aggregate program risk is far greater than any single missing policy: contractual indemnity obligations to multiple counties cannot be met; PE sponsor standards likely cannot be met; balance sheet exposure is substantial. The cure is not a single endorsement but a comprehensive re-marketing of the program.
findings.plain_english: We're missing 9 separate insurance categories. Individually each one is a finding; together they're a structural problem. The right next step is a comprehensive re-marketing of the whole program with a clear scope-of-work, contract abstracts, and exposure profile delivered to several specialty markets at once. That gets you to a coordinated, contract-compliant program faster than fixing one policy at a time.

Scope: WC, Commercial Auto, Umbrella, standalone Cyber, Election Services E&O / Tech E&O, EPLI, D&O / Management Liability, Fiduciary, standalone Crime, PLL. Use the contract requirements (Sacramento + Maricopa + any others active) as the binding spec. Coordinate carrier selection across lines for AI/WoS/P&NC consistency, follow-form Umbrella, and AM Best A-VII minimum (Sacramento threshold). Deliver a binder and complete program summary to PE sponsor and Runbeck CFO within 60 days.

Would the PE sponsor and the CFO be willing to sit through a one-hour program-architecture review based on contract obligations?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation / Material Change Notice — Auto (Gen-1 + Maricopa §8.2.15)
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s) — 30 days written notice (other than non-payment). … Notice does NOT grant or extend rights — informational only. (Form 401-1235 12 14, Pg 44–46). Cancellation Extension under 461-0155 Item 1: 60-day non-payment-excepted cancellation between insurer and named insured.
findings.gap_description: Form 401-1235 12 14 provides 30-day designated-entity NOC for CANCELLATION only — it does not address material changes, suspensions, non-renewals, or scope/limit reductions. Maricopa §8.2.15 expressly requires 30-day notice for ALL of the following triggers: expire, suspend, cancel, or materially change. The endorsement is also informational-only (does not grant or extend rights to the designated entity). Separately, the broker benchmark of 90 days advance notice (Gen-1) is not met — even the carrier-to-named-insured cancellation provision is 60 days.
findings.plain_english: Your county contracts require you to give 30 days advance notice if any insurance is cancelled OR materially changed (limit reduced, scope narrowed, etc.). The endorsement on this auto policy only triggers a notice if the policy is cancelled — it doesn't trigger if the carrier waters down coverage mid-term. If a county finds out coverage was reduced and they weren't notified, they can declare a material breach and terminate the contract.
findings.recommendation: Endorse Form 401-1235 (or successor) to extend notice obligations to material change, suspension, and non-renewal — not just cancellation. Add Maricopa County (Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St Ste 910, Phoenix AZ 85003) and any active Sacramento County contract holders to the designated-entity schedule. Push for 90-day notice on a blanket 'where required by written contract' basis to align with broker best practice. If carrier won't endorse material-change language, the contractor's internal compliance process must catch it — set up a workflow so any midterm endorsement triggers immediate notification to Maricopa.
discoveryQuestions: If your auto carrier sent you a midterm endorsement narrowing coverage on hired & non-owned vehicles, who in your shop would catch it and notify Maricopa within 30 days?
Have you ever had a county pull a contract or place you in default because they weren't told about an insurance change?
Do you know whether the cancellation language on your COIs distinguishes between policy cancellation and material change in coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors & Omissions Giveback (Gen-2)
findings.contract_quote: N/A — Industry best practice; broker RMF item.
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Business Auto Coverage Broadening Endorsement, Item 19: Unintentional Failure to Disclose Hazards.
findings.gap_description: The Hanover Business Auto Broadening Endorsement (461-0155) Item 19 includes an unintentional failure-to-disclose giveback. An inadvertent failure to report a vehicle, location, or operational change cannot be used by the carrier to deny coverage or void the policy.
findings.plain_english: Good news: if your team forgets to add a new vehicle to the policy or fails to report an operational change, your carrier can't deny a claim on that basis alone. This is a meaningful protection, especially for a multi-state services company where vehicle and operational changes are common.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm this giveback is preserved at every renewal and verify equivalent language exists on every other policy in the program (GL, WC, Umbrella, Cyber, etc.).

findings.requirement_type: Named Insureds — Cross-Program Symmetry (Gen-3)
findings.contract_quote: Named Insured — It is best to see the insured's financial report in order to discover all entities. … Does the policy have broad wording to include all subsidiaries? Joint Ventures…
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0174: 'Additional Named Insured Endorsement' schedules: Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc, Runbeck Companies 401(k) Profit Sharing Plan, Lincoln Shields LLC, Black Mountain Investment Co. LLC.
findings.gap_description: Six affiliated entities are scheduled by name on Form 461-0174 — including the four LLCs and the 401(k) plan. This is a reliable inclusion (no Broad Form Named Insured carve-out risk for LLCs). However, this audit lacks visibility into the GL, WC, Umbrella, Cyber, and other program policies — the most common Named-Insured gap in any program is asymmetric scheduling (an entity appears on Auto but not on Umbrella, or appears on GL but not on Cyber). Without those policies in scope, asymmetry cannot be ruled out.
findings.plain_english: All your affiliated entities (the LLCs, the 401(k) plan, the holding companies) are properly listed on the Auto policy by name — that's good and avoids a common gap with LLCs. But we can only see the Auto policy in this review. The most common entity-asymmetry problem is when a sister entity is on the Auto policy but missing from the Umbrella, or on GL but missing from Cyber — meaning a claim against that entity drops to a bare CGL with no umbrella protection. We need to verify the same six entities appear identically across every policy in the program.
findings.recommendation: Pull the Named Insured / Additional Named Insured schedules from every other policy in the program (GL, WC, Umbrella, Cyber, E&O, D&O, Property, Crime) and compare against the 461-0174 schedule on the Auto policy. Any entity scheduled on Auto but missing from another policy is a finding. Also confirm with management: are there any newly formed entities (acquisitions, JVs, real-estate LLCs) since the last renewal that need to be added before they create a coverage gap?

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge — Officer-Limited Endorsement (Gen-4 / CA-13)
findings.contract_quote: Notice & Knowledge — Is the policy wording endorsed so notice of an occurrence is only considered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, and/or the risk manager is notified?
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Business Auto Coverage Broadening Endorsement, Item 17: Knowledge of accident requires notice to executive officer/insurance manager.
findings.gap_description: The Broadening Endorsement (461-0155) Item 17 limits the trigger of 'knowledge of an accident' to the executive officer or insurance manager — preventing a low-level employee's awareness of an incident from being imputed to the company for late-notice coverage denial purposes.
findings.plain_english: Good news: if a driver gets in a fender-bender and doesn't tell anyone for two months, the carrier can't argue 'your company knew about it' just because the driver knew. The policy says only the officer or insurance manager triggers the notice clock. This protects you from a coverage denial based on a low-level employee's failure to report.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Verify equivalent Notice & Knowledge endorsements exist on the GL, WC, Cyber, and E&O policies — this is one of the most common cross-program asymmetries.

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — Blanket (Gen-5 / CA Maricopa §8.2.8 / Sacramento §VIII)
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0500 11 13: 'Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others to Us' — BLANKET WHERE REQUIRED BY WRITTEN CONTRACT. Applies only to extent subrogation waived prior to accident or loss under contract. Reinforced by 461-0155 Item 18 Blanket Waiver preserved through insured contract/written agreement/permit.
findings.gap_description: Auto policy has a blanket Waiver of Subrogation triggered by written contract executed prior to loss. This satisfies both Maricopa §8.2.8 and Sacramento §VIII WoS-on-Auto requirements as well as RMF Gen-5 best practice.
findings.plain_english: Good: your auto carrier has agreed in advance not to come after any county or counterparty you're under contract with after paying a claim — as long as the contract was signed before the accident. No special endorsement is needed each time a new county contract is signed.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm equivalent blanket WoS endorsements exist on the GL, WC (state-specific WC 04 03 06 in CA), and Umbrella policies — this is required by both county contracts.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Additional Insured — Blanket / Primary & Noncontributory (CA-1 / Sacramento §VII / Maricopa §8.2.7)
findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, and volunteers are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: … automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR. … PRIMARY INSURANCE: For any claims related to this Agreement, the CONTRACTOR's insurance coverage shall be endorsed to be primary insurance as respects the COUNTY…
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0478 12 12 'Blanket Additional Insured – Primary and Non-Contributory': Blanket AI when required by written contract/agreement/permit executed before the accident and during policy period. Primary and non-contributory included.
findings.gap_description: Form 461-0478 provides blanket Additional Insured status with Primary and Non-Contributory language, triggered by written contract executed before loss. Auto AI is ongoing-operations only, which is the industry norm for Auto (completed-ops doesn't apply to auto in the same way it does to GL).
findings.plain_english: Good news on the Auto AI: any county or counterparty you have a written contract with automatically becomes an additional insured on your auto policy, and your auto coverage pays first (primary) without diluting their own insurance (non-contributory). You don't need to request a separate endorsement for each county.
findings.recommendation: No action required for Auto AI mechanics. However, see Finding 7 — the AI scope-limitation language in 461-0478 may not satisfy Sacramento's 'no endorsed limitations' requirement.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Additional Insured — 'No Endorsed Limitations' Compliance (Sacramento §VII.A)
findings.contract_quote: The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, or volunteers.
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0478 12 12: 'AI limit is lesser of contract-required or policy limit; … Coverage to AI no broader than coverage provided to any other insured. Exceptions: (1) sole negligence of AI; (2) negligence on non-owned/non-trailer auto by AI/Insured; (3) when AI is AI under another liability policy.'
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.A requires that AI coverage contain NO endorsed limitations on scope of protection. Form 461-0478 contains three notable scope qualifiers: (a) limit reduced to lesser of contract-required or policy limit; (b) 'no broader than … other insured' qualifier; and (c) excess-only treatment if the AI is also an AI under another policy ('other AI exception'). The 'sole negligence of AI' carve-out is acceptable (and aligned with Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b) — see Finding 9), but the 'other AI' qualifier creates a non-contributory disconnect: if the County is also an AI on a co-contractor's policy, this Auto policy could drop to excess instead of being primary as Sacramento §VII.C requires.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires that nothing in your additional-insured language can narrow the County's protection. Your auto AI endorsement has fine-print qualifiers — most importantly, if the County is also additional-insured on a different vendor's policy for the same incident, your auto coverage drops to excess rather than acting as primary. That contradicts Sacramento's primary-and-noncontributory requirement and could be flagged by their Risk Manager during COI review.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate a manuscript or upgraded blanket AI endorsement that (a) does not condition primary status on absence of other AI policies, and (b) does not contain a 'no broader than other insureds' shrinking provision. If Hanover will not amend, prepare a written disclosure to Sacramento Risk Manager alongside any COI explaining the carve-outs and request a waiver — Sacramento §VI.A.1 grants the Risk Manager discretion. The Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b) sole-negligence exception is statutorily required and not a defect.
discoveryQuestions: When you submit COIs to Sacramento County for ballot/election work, has their Risk Manager ever pushed back on AI endorsement language?

Do you ever work alongside other vendors at a county facility where the county might also be an AI on the other vendor's policy — and have you thought about how your insurance interacts with theirs in that scenario?
If a forklift incident at a county warehouse triggered a claim, would you want your $1M auto policy to pay first dollar or sit excess of someone else's coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Auto Severability of Interest / Separation of Insureds (Sacramento §VII.D)
findings.contract_quote: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.
findings.policy_quote: CA 00 01 03 06 Business Auto Coverage Form §IV.B: 'Except with respect to the Limit of Insurance, the coverage afforded applies separately to each insured who is seeking coverage or against whom a 'claim' is made or 'suit' is brought.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO Business Auto Coverage Form CA 00 01 03 06 contains the Separation of Insureds condition that satisfies Sacramento §VII.D. No special endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: Good: the standard auto policy form already treats each insured (you, your affiliates, the county as AI) as if they had their own separate policy when a claim is made. This is built into the form — no extra endorsement needed.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: California Civil Code §2782(b) Carve-Out (Sacramento §VII.B)
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: 461-0478 12 12 Exception: 'sole negligence of AI' — coverage does not apply to bodily injury or property damage caused by sole negligence of any additional insured.
findings.gap_description: The 461-0478 sole-negligence carve-out aligns with the California Civil Code §2782(b) public-policy limit on AI coverage for active negligence. No conflict with Sacramento §VII.B.
findings.plain_english: Good: California has a public-policy rule that says you can't insure another party for their OWN active negligence — your policy reflects that. Sacramento County acknowledges this in their contract, so this is contractually compliant.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Liability Limit — Sacramento $1M CSL (req-003)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000 (per declarations). Hired Auto Liability: included (cost of hire basis, AZ class 6611). Non-Owned Auto Liability: included (55 employees, AZ class 6602).
findings.policy_page: Pg 26–27 (Item Three / Item Four / Item Five schedules)
findings.gap_description: Auto policy carries $1M CSL with hired and non-owned coverage included. Meets Sacramento §III.B exactly.
findings.plain_english: Good: your $1M auto liability with hired and non-owned coverage exactly meets Sacramento County's minimum. No shortfall.
findings.recommendation: No action required for Sacramento. (See Finding 11 — Maricopa County requires $2M, which is a different story.)

findings.requirement_type: Auto Liability Limit — Maricopa $2M CSL Shortfall (req-010)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000.
findings.policy_page: Pg 26 (Item Three Schedule of Covered Autos)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires $2M CSL on commercial auto. This policy carries $1M CSL — a $1M shortfall on the underlying. Whether this shortfall is cured by an umbrella depends on (a) whether an umbrella exists (not in scope of this audit) and (b) interpretation of Maricopa §8.2.9 (program-level umbrella permission) versus §8.2.11 (Auto clause does not inline-mention umbrella) — see Finding 12.
findings.plain_english: Bad gap: Maricopa County requires $2 million on auto. You have $1 million. If a county vehicle gets hit at full speed by your Sprinter or Express van, the damages could easily exceed $1M, and Maricopa could declare you in material breach for not meeting their minimum. Whether your umbrella fixes this depends on whether (i) you have an umbrella in your program (we couldn't see one in this review), (ii) it actually attaches to auto, and (iii) Maricopa's Risk Manager accepts umbrella as fulfilling the per-line $2M requirement.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) increase auto CSL to $2M on the underlying policy at renewal — relatively cheap incremental premium for a 2-vehicle fleet; OR (b) confirm an umbrella is in place that attaches over auto with at least $1M of additional limit and obtain written acknowledgement from Maricopa Risk Manager that umbrella attachment satisfies §8.2.11. Option (a) is cleaner and avoids the §8.2.11 interpretive ambiguity entirely.
discoveryQuestions: When you bid Maricopa County work, did anyone in their procurement office flag the $2M auto requirement, or did they accept the COI as-is?
Your Sprinter and Express van are both used to deliver ballots — what's the worst-case scenario you've imagined for an at-fault accident with one of them?
Do you have an umbrella policy, and if so, do you know whether it stacks over auto or whether Maricopa's risk team would accept that stacking?
What's the cost differential between $1M and $2M auto CSL — has anyone quoted it for you?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Umbrella Attachment to Auto — Interpretive Ambiguity
findings.contract_quote: [§8.2.9] If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. … [§8.2.11] Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit … of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence …
findings.policy_quote: Auto policy CSL: $1,000,000. Umbrella policy: NOT IN SCOPE OF THIS AUDIT.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 grants program-level permission to use umbrella to meet minimum limits. §8.2.11 (Auto) does NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment, in contrast to §8.2.10 (CGL) which expressly says 'CGL … and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance.' Strict reading: umbrella may not satisfy auto minimum because §8.2.11 omits the inline reference. Permissive reading: §8.2.9 program-level permission applies to all required policies including auto. Outcome depends on Maricopa Risk Manager's interpretation.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract has two clauses that say slightly different things about whether an umbrella can fill in for the underlying auto limit. The general clause says yes; the auto clause doesn't repeat that promise. We can't tell you which way Maricopa will read it without asking them — and an interpretive ambiguity at claim time is a bad place to find yourself.
findings.recommendation: Get Maricopa Risk Management's written interpretation BEFORE the next contract performance period. If they confirm umbrella stacking is acceptable for auto (per §8.2.9 program-level permission), document it in writing and keep on file. If they require $2M on the underlying auto policy specifically, fix Finding 11 by raising auto CSL to $2M. Do NOT rely on umbrella to silently cure the gap without confirmation.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Deductible/SIR Allocation — Auto $1,000 Deductibles vs. §8.2.6 (req-005)
findings.contract_quote: Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Comprehensive Deductible: $1,000. Collision Deductible: $1,000.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.6 requires that deductibles/SIRs NOT apply with respect to coverage provided to the County. The Hanover Auto policy has $1,000 comp/collision deductibles; standard policy form does not contain a 'deductible waived as respects additional insured' endorsement. Auto deductibles only apply to physical damage on owned autos (not third-party liability), so the practical exposure is limited — but technically the contract requires the deductible structure not to affect the County. This may also create an obligation for Run-Test to disclose deductibles per Sacramento §IV.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says any deductibles can't reduce what the County gets paid. Your auto deductibles are small ($1,000) and only apply to your own vehicle damage, not to liability claims by the County — so the practical risk is small. But Maricopa technically reserves the right to demand a surety bond or letter of credit backing your deductibles, and they could ask you to disclose them at any time. Worth declaring upfront.
findings.recommendation: Disclose deductibles to Maricopa Risk Management proactively (per Sacramento §IV, also disclose to Sacramento Risk Manager). Maintain documentation that auto deductibles only apply to physical damage on owned autos and do not impair third-party liability indemnification of the County. If Maricopa pushes back, evaluate whether a small Letter of Credit ($2,000 covering both deductibles) is the path of least resistance.
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa or any other county ever asked for a Letter of Credit or surety bond backing your insurance deductibles?
When you submit COIs, do you proactively disclose deductibles, or only when asked?
If you had to post a $5,000 LOC or bond to satisfy a county risk manager, would that be a problem operationally?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier A.M. Best Rating — A-VII / B++ (Sacramento req-016 / Maricopa req-002)
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento] Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. [Maricopa] … possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1, Page 3 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.1, Page 5 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Allmerica Financial Benefit Insurance Company (The Hanover Insurance Group).
findings.gap_description: Allmerica Financial Benefit (Hanover Insurance Group subsidiary) carries an A.M. Best rating of A (Excellent), Financial Size Category XV (over $2 billion in policyholder surplus). This exceeds both the Sacramento A-VII threshold and the Maricopa B++ threshold by comfortable margins. Verify current rating at renewal — A.M. Best ratings can change.
findings.plain_english: Good: your auto carrier is rated well above what either Sacramento or Maricopa requires. No carrier-rating concern on auto.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Allmerica's current A.M. Best rating annually at renewal. Verify the same standard is met on every other policy in the program — non-admitted/E&S placements often fall below A-VII even when financially adequate.

findings.requirement_type: Auto BI Definition — Mental Anguish (CA-2)
findings.contract_quote: Bodily injury including Mental Anguish?
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Business Auto Coverage Broadening Endorsement, Item 21: Mental anguish included in BI.

findings.plain_english: Good: mental anguish counts as bodily injury under your auto policy. If a passenger is unhurt physically but suffers PTSD or significant emotional trauma after an accident, that's covered.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Verify the same Mental Anguish-in-BI extension exists on the GL policy.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Broad Named Insured + Newly Acquired Entities (CA-3)
findings.contract_quote: Broad Named Insured as well as all Named Insureds all listed.
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 3: Broadened Named Insured for newly acquired/formed entities. 461-0174: Six affiliated entities scheduled by name (Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc, Runbeck Companies 401(k) Profit Sharing Plan, Lincoln Shields LLC, Black Mountain Investment Co. LLC).
findings.gap_description: Named insured structure is comprehensive: existing affiliates listed by name on a schedule (avoiding any LLC carve-out risk that often plagues 'Broad Form Named Insured' wording), and newly acquired entities are auto-added by 461-0155 Item 3.
findings.plain_english: Good: every affiliated company is listed by name, including all the LLCs (which often get accidentally excluded by generic 'broad form' wording). Plus, if you acquire or form a new entity midterm, it's automatically added to the policy without you having to call your broker.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the Broadened Named Insured time limit and disclosure requirements (newly acquired entities typically must be reported within 30/60/90 days). Verify the same six entities are scheduled identically across all other policies in the program.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Lease Gap Coverage (CA-4)
findings.contract_quote: Lease Gap coverage.
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 15: Auto Loan/Lease Gap. Item 16: Auto Lease Physical Damage. Item 11: $1,000/day lessor loss of use up to 7 days.

Loan/Lease Gap and Auto Lease Physical Damage coverage is in force via the Broadening Endorsement — protects against the difference between book value and lease/loan balance in a total-loss scenario.
findings.plain_english: Good: if either van is totaled, the policy will pay the actual cash value PLUS the gap between that and your loan balance — you won't be stuck owing money on a vehicle that no longer exists. Even though both vans appear to be owned, this protection is in place if any future vehicles are leased or financed.

findings.requirement_type: Drive Other Car (DOC) Coverage (CA-5)
findings.contract_quote: Drive Other Car - Including no-fault as applicable? You would like this cover on the broadest basis possible.
findings.policy_quote: Form CA 99 10 (Drive Other Car) NOT identified in endorsement schedule.
findings.gap_description: Drive Other Car (DOC) endorsement is typically used when executive officers or principals drive personal vehicles for business or do not own personal autos and rely on company coverage as primary. DOC provides liability and physical damage as if the named individual had a personal auto policy. The Auto policy schedule does not list a DOC endorsement; whether one is needed depends on whether named-insured executives (e.g., CEO, CFO) operate personal vehicles for business and lack their own personal auto policy.
findings.plain_english: DOC coverage is for executives who drive personal cars on company business — it acts like a personal auto policy when the company auto policy doesn't apply. We can't tell from the policy whether you have any executives who need this. If officers regularly use personal vehicles for company errands, this is a gap worth fixing.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with management: do any officers/principals drive personal vehicles for business and rely on company coverage? If yes, add CA 99 10 Drive Other Car endorsement scheduling those individuals. If no (officers carry their own personal auto policies and only use company vehicles for company business), this is N/A.

findings.requirement_type: Employee as Insured (CA 9933) + Employee Hired Auto (CA 2054) (CA-6)
findings.contract_quote: Employee as Insured's CA 9933 & Employee Hired Autos CA 2054.
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 2: Employee Hired Autos under Symbol 8 (broader Hanover proprietary version of CA 2054). Item 4: Employees as Insureds when using non-owned/non-hired autos in business (broader version of CA 9933).
findings.gap_description: Both Employee Hired Auto and Employee as Insured coverages are embedded in 461-0155, providing equivalent or broader protection than ISO CA 2054 and CA 9933. Important for an election services company where employees may rent vehicles or use personal cars to deliver ballots in 31 states.
findings.plain_english: Good: when an employee rents a vehicle on the company's behalf or uses their personal car for company business (e.g., delivering ballots), they're treated as insureds under the policy. Without these coverages, the employee personally bears liability for accidents in those scenarios.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Educate field employees that their personal auto policy is excess to the company auto policy when driving for business — and that they should still notify their personal carrier of business use to avoid coverage disputes.

findings.requirement_type: Limited Pollution Endorsement — Auto (CA-8 / CA 99 48)
findings.contract_quote: Environmental Exposures - are there any? Does the policy include the limited pollution endorsement as a minimum?
findings.policy_quote: CA 00 01 03 06 Pollution Exclusion (with auto-fluids carve-back): 'Excludes pollution from cargo or pollutants in transit. Carve-back preserves coverage for fuels/lubricants/exhaust gases needed for normal functioning of the auto, and for accidents away from owned/rented premises caused by upset/overturn of a covered auto.'
findings.gap_description: Standard CA 00 01 form has the pollution exclusion with the standard carve-back for fluids needed for vehicle operation and for upset/overturn accidents. The CA 99 48 Pollution Liability — Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos endorsement is NOT identified on the schedule. CA 99 48 provides expanded pollution coverage for cargo-related discharge and broader pollutants-in-transit scenarios. For an election services manufacturer that primarily transports paper ballots and election equipment (low pollution exposure), the standard form may be sufficient — but if any vehicles transport printer toner, ink in bulk, batteries for ballot scanners, or any chemical inventory between locations, CA 99 48 may be warranted.
findings.plain_english: If your vans only carry paper ballots and finished election equipment, the standard pollution carve-back (covering fuel/oil leaks from the van itself) is probably enough. But if you ever transport bulk printer toner, ink, battery banks, or any chemicals — even in small commercial quantities — there's a gap because cargo pollution from upset/overturn is excluded. We need to know what's actually in those vans.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with operations: what's loaded in the Sprinter and Express on a typical run? If only ballots and election hardware, the current carve-back is sufficient. If any chemical inventory (printer toner/ink in bulk, battery banks for ballot scanners, cleaning supplies in commercial quantities), endorse CA 99 48 Pollution Liability — Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos.

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Exclusion — Auto (CA-9)
findings.contract_quote: Fellow Employee Exclusion, is it deleted? Does the insured want it deleted?

This is the recommended structure: WC/EL stays primary for employee-on-employee injury claims, but the auto policy provides excess protection if WC/EL is exhausted or denied.
findings.plain_english: Good: if one of your employees driving the Sprinter injures another employee who's a passenger, your Workers' Comp pays first (which is what should happen). But if WC limits run out or there's a dispute about whether the injury was work-related, the auto policy steps in as backup. Without this amendment, the auto policy would simply deny — leaving the employee with no path to recovery beyond WC.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm WC/EL limits are adequate as the primary line.

findings.requirement_type: No-Fault State Operations Review (CA-11)
findings.contract_quote: For vehicles in no-fault states has the insured ever been presented all the optional coverage with the pros and cons?
findings.policy_quote: Two covered autos garaged in AZ (a tort state). No PIP / no-fault election forms identified for other states.

If your AZ-registered vans ever drive into Florida, New York, Pennsylvania, etc. for ballot work, you may have a statutory PIP gap. The carrier typically extends PIP automatically when the vehicle enters those states, but it's worth confirming.

findings.requirement_type: Mobile Equipment vs. Auto Definition (CA-12)

findings.policy_quote: Two covered autos scheduled (Mercedes Sprinter, Chevrolet Express). 461-0178 Miscellaneous Coverages — Broadening: vehicle 950, AZ class 124, comprehensive only with $500 limit/deductible. Symbol 1 vs. Symbol 7 analysis not in scope of available data.
findings.gap_description: Election services manufacturers may use forklifts, scissor lifts, ballot equipment carts, generators, or printing-line mobile equipment that may or may not be subject to motor vehicle laws. Some such equipment falls under the GL policy's mobile equipment definition; some (e.g., self-propelled equipment with mounted permanent equipment) may be 'auto' under state vehicle code and require auto liability scheduling. The 461-0178 Miscellaneous Coverages endorsement schedules a single 'vehicle 950' with $500 comprehensive only — likely a piece of equipment, not a road vehicle. Without facility/operations review, mobile equipment scheduling cannot be confirmed.
findings.plain_english: Manufacturers often have forklifts, scissor lifts, sweeper trucks, and similar equipment that look like 'mobile equipment' under your GL policy but may legally be 'autos' under state law if they go on public roads. If a piece of equipment is misclassified, a claim could fall in a gap between GL and Auto. We can't tell from the policy alone whether you have any of this — needs a facility walkthrough.
findings.recommendation: Conduct a fleet/equipment walkthrough at the Phoenix facility. List every piece of self-propelled or towed equipment and confirm with the broker whether it's properly classified as auto, mobile equipment under GL, or scheduled equipment under Inland Marine. findings.recommendation: Confirm vehicle title for both VINs. If both are titled to Runbeck Election Services Inc, no action required. If either is personally owned or leased from an employee, add CA 99 16 or CA 99 47 as appropriate.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Symbols Analysis — Symbol 1/2 vs. Symbol 7 (CA-16)
findings.contract_quote: Symbols - you are looking for 1 and 2 versus 7. Additionally are there any examples of mobile equipment that are subject to any motor vehicle law that needs to be scheduled? Also, please note that symbols 2,8&9 are not equivalent to symbol 1.
findings.policy_quote: Symbol assignments not explicitly visible in available policy data. Hired Auto Liability rated under Symbol 8 (per 461-0155 Item 2 enhancement). Employer's Non-Ownership Liability under Symbol 9. Owned auto symbol assignment (1, 2, or 7) not confirmed in available text.
findings.policy_page: Schedule of Coverages page (not in available extracts)
findings.gap_description: Symbol 1 ('any auto') is the broadest auto liability symbol — covering owned, leased, hired, and non-owned autos under one trigger. Symbol 7 limits to specifically described autos. Symbol 2 limits to all owned autos but excludes non-owned/hired (which are picked up by Symbols 8 and 9 separately). For a manufacturer with growing operations and 55 employees with potential personal-vehicle business use, Symbol 1 for liability is preferred. The available policy data does not confirm whether Liability is on Symbol 1 or a narrower symbol.
findings.plain_english: Auto policies use 'symbols' to describe what's covered. Symbol 1 is 'any auto' — the broadest coverage. Other symbols are narrower. We can't confirm from the available data whether your policy uses Symbol 1 (best) or a narrower symbol. The difference matters: if a non-listed vehicle gets used for company work and the policy uses Symbol 7, you may have no coverage.
findings.recommendation: Confirm symbol assignments on the Schedule of Coverages page. Liability should be Symbol 1 (any auto). Physical damage typically uses Symbol 7 (specifically described autos) for cost reasons — that's normal. If liability is on a symbol other than 1, request a change.

findings.requirement_type: Temporary & Leased Workers — 'Employee' Definition (CA-17)

findings.gap_description: Election services manufacturers often hire temporary/seasonal workers during election cycles to handle ballot processing, mail sorting, and equipment deployment. The policy data does not show an endorsement modifying the employee definition.
findings.plain_english: Election cycles spike your headcount with temps. If those temps are technically employees of a staffing agency, the auto policy may treat them as 'fellow employees' for exclusion purposes — meaning if a Run-Test driver injures a temp in a vehicle, the temp's BI claim could be denied under the fellow-employee exclusion. We need to confirm how your staffing arrangements are structured and whether the auto policy's employee definition needs adjusting.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with HR/operations: are temps direct W-2 hires of Run-Test, or sourced through a PEO/staffing agency? If staffing agency: (a) request the Alternate Employer Endorsement on the staffing agency's WC policy, AND (b) endorse the auto policy to exclude leased workers from the 'employee' definition so the Fellow Employee Exclusion does not bar coverage for injuries to temps caused by a Run-Test driver.

findings.requirement_type: Uninsured / Underinsured Motorists — Coverage and Election (CA-18)
findings.contract_quote: Uninsured / Underinsured - Does the Insured understand what they are buying and how much it costs…

findings.recommendation: Pull the executed AZ UM/UIM Selection Form (461-0368) from the carrier and confirm the elections were made at $1M. File the executed form. Educate management that UM/UIM does NOT pay punitive damages and excludes claims settled without insurer consent.

findings.requirement_type: Excluded Driver — Malina Trujillo (461-0425)
findings.contract_quote: Excludes coverage for any 'accident' or 'loss' resulting from operation/use of any covered auto by Malina Trujillo (with exception of UM/UIM).
findings.contract_page: 461-0425 (9/10) Arizona Exclusion of Named Driver, Pg 8
findings.policy_quote: Excludes coverage for any 'accident' or 'loss' resulting from operation/use of any covered auto by Malina Trujillo (with exception of UM/UIM).

If they ever drive one of your vans, even once, any accident is on your company directly with no insurance backstop. (2) If yes, document in writing (HR file + driver authorization log) that Trujillo is prohibited from operating any company vehicle. (3) If Trujillo is no longer employed, ask Hanover to remove the exclusion endorsement at the next renewal. (4) If the underlying MVR concern can be remedied (e.g., expungement of violations, time elapsed), seek removal of exclusion sooner.

Have you reviewed MVRs for everyone who might drive a company vehicle, including non-fleet employees who occasionally use the vans?

findings.requirement_type: Cargo / Customer Property in Transit — Coverage Gap
findings.contract_quote: Care, Custody or Control Exclusion: Excludes property damage to property in insured's care, custody or control or transported by insured. Carve-back for sidetrack agreement only. Cargo/property of others while in transit (e.g., customer ballots/equipment) is NOT covered under Auto Liability.
findings.policy_quote: Care, Custody or Control Exclusion (CA 00 01 §II.B.6): excludes property damage to property in insured's care, custody, or control or transported by insured.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports COUNTY-OWNED property — printed ballots, ballot scanners, election technology hardware — between the Phoenix facility and customer sites in 31 states. The Auto policy's CCC exclusion bars coverage for damage to property in transit on a covered auto. This is exactly the kind of cargo loss that requires an Inland Marine / Motor Truck Cargo policy. Without IM in place, a fire in the Sprinter destroying a county's ballots and ballot scanners is uninsured — and the indemnification obligations under the Maricopa MSA §8.1 and Sacramento §VII would expose Run-Test directly.
findings.plain_english: This is a real exposure. Your vans transport ballots, ballot scanners, and county-owned election technology. If the Sprinter catches fire on I-10 and destroys $400,000 of county property, your auto policy WILL NOT pay — there's an explicit exclusion for property in your care being transported by you. You'd be on the hook directly to the county under your indemnity obligations. This needs an Inland Marine policy or Motor Truck Cargo policy specifically.
findings.recommendation: Verify whether an Inland Marine or Motor Truck Cargo policy is in the program (this audit only sees the Auto policy). If yes, confirm: (a) covered property includes customer property in care/custody/control during transit, (b) limits are adequate for max single-load value (likely $250K–$1M per vehicle for ballot/equipment runs), (c) waiver of subrogation in favor of counties is endorsed (per Sacramento §IX). If no IM in program, this is an Ugly uninsured exposure and a standalone policy is required immediately.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Inland Marine / Motor Truck Cargo (if in program — verify)
discoveryQuestions: When you ship ballots and ballot scanners to a county for an election, who legally owns that property during transit — the county or Run-Test?
What's the highest-dollar load you've ever had in one of your vans on a single run?
If your Sprinter caught fire and destroyed a county's ballots three days before an election, who pays — you, the county, or insurance?
Do you have an Inland Marine or Motor Truck Cargo policy, and have you ever read what the limits and exclusions are?

findings.requirement_type: TRIA / Terrorism — Auto (CGL-32 analog applied to Auto)
findings.contract_quote: Tria - Does the insured buy terrorism and has it been explained thoroughly.
findings.policy_quote: CA 23 85 01 06 'Exclusion of Terrorism Involving Nuclear, Biological or Chemical Terrorism' — excludes only NBC terrorism. Conventional terrorism remains covered. 461-0301 01 07 Notice to Policyholder on Terrorism — federal TRIA does not apply to commercial auto.
findings.gap_description: Federal TRIA does not apply to commercial auto. The Hanover Auto policy excludes only nuclear/biological/chemical (NBC) terrorism — conventional terrorism (e.g., a vehicle attack at an election event) remains covered under the standard auto liability form. However, the NBC exclusion is meaningful for an election services company: dispersal of biological/chemical agents at a polling location served by Run-Test could be alleged as a 'terrorism' event triggering exclusion. There is no separate stand-alone terrorism policy identified in this audit scope.
findings.plain_english: Election work is a terrorism target, full stop. Your auto policy still covers a conventional vehicle attack (someone driving into a crowd). What it doesn't cover is a chemical/biological/nuclear event — and unlike GL, federal TRIA doesn't backstop auto. If a polling location your van delivered ballots to is attacked with a biological agent, there's a real argument the auto exposure flowing from that incident has no coverage. Worth a conversation about whether a separate terrorism placement makes sense.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm with management whether a stand-alone terrorism / political violence policy is in the program. (2) If not, consider whether the heightened exposure profile of election services — voter rolls, ballot facilities, drop-off points — warrants a stand-alone terrorism policy that can include conventional + NBC + active assailant + cyber-terrorism. (3) Document a board-level decision to retain or transfer the NBC terrorism exposure given the federal TRIA gap on auto.
discoveryQuestions: Election infrastructure is a stated DHS Critical Infrastructure target — has your board discussed whether a stand-alone terrorism policy makes sense given that designation?
If a biological agent were dispersed at a polling location your team had just serviced, do you know whether your insurance would respond?
Have you ever been asked by a county to demonstrate active assailant or terrorism coverage as part of a security review?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Subcontractor Pass-Through (req-012)

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Split Limits / Tiered Coverage by Wrongful Act Date
findings.contract_quote: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Split Limits of Liability (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #4): (a) Wrongful Acts on or after 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate; (b) Acts on or after 09/06/2019: additional $1M xs $1M; (c) Acts on or after 04/01/2021: additional $3M xs $2M. Effective full $5M/$5M only available for Wrongful Acts first committed on or after 04/01/2021. Wrongful Acts committed between 12/1/2007 and 09/05/2019 are limited to $1M/$1M.
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #4 replaces the policy's stated $5M/$5M limits with a tiered structure pegged to when the underlying Wrongful Act was 'first committed.' Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history and a stated retro of 3/27/2017. A claim alleging a Wrongful Act first committed before 09/06/2019 — even if the claim is reported in the 2025-26 policy year — has only $1M of coverage available from the primary, not $5M. The Convex excess sits over the $5M attachment point, so a Wrongful Act first committed pre-2019 leaves a $4M gap between the $1M primary cap and the $5M Convex attachment that NEITHER policy responds to.
findings.plain_english: On paper you have $10M of E&O. In reality, if a county sues you over something your team did before September 2019, your coverage drops to $1M and there's a $4M dead zone before the excess kicks in. Election operations have long-tail exposure — a ballot processing error from 2018 could surface in a 2026 audit or recount challenge. This is the single biggest hidden gap in the program.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate with Gemini at renewal to: (1) collapse the split-limits endorsement so all covered Wrongful Acts attach to the full $5M tower; or (2) at minimum, advance the Tier (a) cap from $1M to match Tier (c). If carrier refuses, consider repricing with a competing market — multiple Tech E&O carriers will write election-services at unified $5M limits. Also confirm the $4M layer gap (between $1M primary cap and $5M Convex attachment) is communicated to ownership/PE sponsor as a residual exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Convex Excess only attaches above $5M and follows form, so it inherits the split-limits cap on pre-2019 acts.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test has been processing ballots for over 50 years. If a county opened a claim today over a ballot or signature-verification issue from your 2017 or 2018 work, do you know how much coverage would actually respond?
Has your prior broker walked you through the difference between the $5M shown on your dec page and the tiered structure inside Endorsement #4?

findings.policy_quote: Media Extension Endorsement (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #5), exclusion W.: 'Client Print Media — Claims by clients of the Insured if the Claim is a result of print media or Content furnished by the client.'
findings.gap_description: The Media Extension endorsement adds a 'Client Print Media' exclusion that bars coverage for any client-brought claim arising from print media or Content furnished by that same client. In Run-Test's business model, counties almost universally furnish ballot content, voter data files, candidate lists, and contest layouts — Run-Test prints what the county supplies. If a county sues Run-Test because a printed ballot was wrong (even where the underlying content error originated with the county's data), this exclusion could be triggered to bar coverage.
findings.plain_english: Counties send you the ballot content. You print it. If a county later sues you over a ballot error, the policy contains a clause that says claims by clients arising from content the client itself supplied are excluded. That's nearly every claim scenario in your operating model. This isn't a corner case — it's the front door of your professional liability exposure.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — request that Gemini delete the Client Print Media exclusion (W.) or carve it back so it only applies where the Insured had no role in formatting, processing, or quality-control of the client-furnished content. Document the workflow: counties supply data, but Run-Test's processes (formatting, layout, validation, print integrity, mail merge) are the value-add. Without a carve-back, the bulk of foreseeable claims could be denied. If Gemini will not budge, this becomes a market-replacement conversation at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through a typical ballot job — when a county sends you their ballot file, how much of the content is theirs versus what your team formats, validates, or proofs?
Has a county ever come back to you after an election and pointed at something that was wrong on a printed ballot? When that happened, was the source data theirs or yours?

If a county sued you tomorrow over a ballot error, would your team be able to prove the formatting and processing work was your independent professional service rather than just a reproduction of what they supplied?
Did anyone explain Endorsement #5 'Client Print Media' exclusion to you when this policy was bound?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Delay in Performance/Delivery Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... [policies] shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.policy_quote: Amendatory Endorsement — Technology Services Extension (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #6), exclusion D.: '[Excludes] Delay in performance or delivery of Technology Products, Technology Services, or any contractual obligation.'
findings.gap_description: The Tech Services endorsement adds a Delay in Performance exclusion that bars claims arising from delayed delivery of any Technology Product, Technology Service, OR any contractual obligation. Election services run on hard statutory deadlines (ballot mailing windows, Federal Post Card Application deadlines for UOCAVA, certification dates). A delayed ballot mailing causing voter disenfranchisement, a county election deadline miss, or contractual liquidated damages for late delivery are ALL foreseeable claim scenarios — and ALL excluded.
findings.plain_english: Your business runs on statutory deadlines that don't move. If you miss a mailing date or a delivery deadline and a county sues for the resulting harm, your E&O policy says delay claims are excluded. This is the most predictable claim trigger in your industry, and it's specifically excluded.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate carve-back to the Delay exclusion at renewal — at minimum, exclude only delays caused by force majeure or insured-controlled willful misconduct, NOT all delays. Run-Test's underwriter should understand election deadline pressure. Failing carve-back, this is a top-tier replacement priority. In the interim, ensure operations team has bulletproof contractual force-majeure protections AND that any liquidated-damages clauses in county contracts are reviewed by counsel for proportionality.
discoveryQuestions: What's the worst-case scenario if you miss a ballot mailing window for a county on a tight deadline — how would that show up financially?
Have your county contracts ever had liquidated damages or penalty clauses tied to delivery dates? Have any been triggered?
When you priced this E&O policy, was the carrier briefed on the deadline-driven nature of election work?
If a county sued you for damages from a late ballot delivery causing voter disenfranchisement, how would you defend that without policy support for delay claims?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Notice & Knowledge Officer-Limited Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §4 — Notice and Knowledge of Claims: 'Is the policy endorsed so that a covered occurrence is only triggered when the company's officer, the person responsible for insurance, the risk manager, or equivalent is notified — rather than ANY employee's knowledge being imputed to the entity?'
findings.policy_quote: Claim Reporting Provision (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #3): 'Notice trigger limited to awareness by CEO, CFO, General Counsel, or Risk Manager (rather than any Insured). Outside notice still capped at 60 days post-Policy Period.'
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #3 properly limits notice imputation to the four executive functions (CEO, CFO, GC, RM). A line employee's awareness of a potential matter does NOT trigger reporting obligations or void coverage.
findings.plain_english: If a customer-service rep hears about a complaint and doesn't escalate, that won't void your coverage — only awareness at the executive level triggers the reporting clock. This is best-practice language and is correctly in place on the E&O.
findings.recommendation: No action required on this policy. Audit other policies in the program (CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, Cyber) for equivalent Notice & Knowledge endorsements; this is a program-level RMF item that should be consistent across all liability policies.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Hammer Clause (Consent to Settle)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL §13 — Duty to Defend / consent-to-settle review.
findings.policy_quote: Consent to Settle Amendment — Miscellaneous (VP 08 51 05 17, End. #16): 'If Insured refuses recommended settlement, carrier liability capped at recommended amount + 80% of subsequent Claim Expenses and Loss. Insured retains 20% of post-refusal costs/loss.'
findings.gap_description: Standard 80/20 hammer clause — if the Insured refuses the carrier's recommended settlement, the Insured bears 20% of every defense dollar and indemnity dollar after the refusal point. Best-in-class hammers are 90/10 or full consent-to-settle (no hammer); 80/20 is mid-market language.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier wants to settle a claim and you don't (because, for example, settlement implies fault on a politically charged election matter), you'll be on the hook for 20% of everything spent after that point — defense costs, judgment, settlement. For a high-value election lawsuit that 20% can be material.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request 90/10 hammer or full consent-to-settle (no hammer). Election-services claims often have reputational considerations that argue against early settlement — a stronger consent provision protects the insured's strategic interests. If carrier won't move from 80/20, document this as a known constraint in claims-management protocols.
discoveryQuestions: If a county brought a claim that implied election fraud or vote-tampering, would you want the option to fight rather than settle even if the carrier recommended a payment?
Has a prior claim ever put you in a position where the carrier wanted to settle but you wanted to defend on principle?
How would your PE sponsor react if a $2M settlement was recommended but you decided to fight and ended up paying 20% of an even larger judgment?

findings.recommendation: No action on the E&O. The architectural cleanliness is appropriate. Cyber adequacy must be solved on the AmTrust policy itself.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Definition of Professional Services (Election-Specific)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Professional Services definition (VP 02 75 07 17, End. #9): 'Solely in the performance as an Election Services Firm including but not limited to: Election ballot services, printing ballot services, election printing, petition printing and services, election and petition design, ballot fulfillment, election hardware and software maintenance, support and technical services, outbound and inbound mail processing services, and election & petition products and services.'
findings.gap_description: The Professional Services definition is custom-tailored to Run-Test's actual operations rather than relying on generic 'tech services' or 'consulting' wording. This is the single most important provision on a Professional Liability policy and is correctly drafted.
findings.plain_english: The policy specifically says it covers 'Election Services Firm' work, naming ballot printing, election design, mail processing, hardware/software support — basically what you actually do. This is a strong, well-tailored definition.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. If any new service lines are added (e.g., voting machine logistics, signature-verification AI, voter outreach analytics), confirm Endorsement #9's enumeration is updated to include them.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Hardware Malfunction & Electrical Failure Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Tech Services Extension (End. #6) exclusions A. & B.: 'Excludes hardware malfunction/defect and electrical failure UNLESS solely caused by Insured's Wrongful Act/negligence.'
findings.gap_description: The carve-back requiring 'solely caused' by Insured's Wrongful Act is unusually narrow. In any concurrent-cause scenario (e.g., a power surge plus an Insured configuration error), the carrier can invoke the exclusion because the Insured cause was not 'sole.' Election technology — printers, scanners, DRE units, ballot-on-demand systems — operates in environments with multiple potential failure causes.
findings.plain_english: If your equipment fails and contributes to a claim, the policy only covers it if your team's action was the SOLE cause. Realistic election-day failures (e.g., heat causes printer jam at the same time a software update is rolled out) involve multiple factors — and that 'solely' word can be used to deny.
findings.recommendation: Push to broaden the carve-back from 'solely' to 'caused in whole or in part' by an Insured Wrongful Act. Standard market language uses concurrent-cause-friendly wording.
discoveryQuestions: How often does election-day equipment failure involve a single root cause versus a combination of environmental, software, and operator factors?
If a printer jams and a software bug both contribute to a delay, would your team be able to definitively say which one 'solely' caused the problem?
Has your incident-response process ever involved root-cause analysis where the answer was genuinely contested?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Self-Insured Retention Disclosure & County Approval

County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit. (Maricopa §8.2.6)

findings.policy_quote: Self-Insured Retention (VP 06 99 07 17, End. #11): 'Self-Insured Retention of $25,000 per claim. Insured must pay SIR for both Loss and Claim Expenses BEFORE carrier has any obligation. Carrier has no duty to defend until SIR exhausted.'
findings.gap_description: The $25K SIR is meaningful structurally — it's a true SIR (insured retains defense within retention using panel counsel) rather than a deductible. Need confirmation that (a) all active county contracts have approved this SIR in writing, and (b) no county has yet exercised the bond/LOC option.
findings.plain_english: You have a $25,000 retention before the policy responds. Both Sacramento and Maricopa require you to disclose and get written approval for that retention. We need to confirm that's been done for every active county contract — and that no county has demanded you post a bond or letter of credit to back it.
findings.recommendation: Pull all active county contracts and their COI approvals; confirm the $25K SIR was disclosed and approved in writing for each. If any contract is silent, push the disclosure now to avoid arguing it post-claim. For Maricopa specifically, monitor for any Risk Manager request to bond/LOC the SIR.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Communicable Disease Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Communicable Disease Exclusion (VP 09 68 04 20, End. #20): 'Absolute exclusion for any Claim alleging/arising out of/attributable to any actual or alleged Communicable Disease — including supervisory/hiring/training acts, testing failures, prevention failures, reporting failures, and related communications.'
findings.gap_description: Post-COVID standard exclusion — broad enough to capture any communicable-disease tangential claim (e.g., a poll worker's exposure complaint, a ballot drop-box hygiene allegation, a voter's claim that mail-in processing failed to follow public health protocols).
findings.plain_english: If a future health emergency causes anyone to allege Run-Test failed to properly handle ballots, mailings, or facilities in a disease-safe way, the policy is silent. Low likelihood in normal years, but cannot be eliminated for an election-cycle company that touches public-facing operations.
findings.recommendation: Note as a known program-wide exclusion (industry-standard since 2020). Document in operational protocols that pandemic-related claim scenarios sit on the company's balance sheet. Revisit at renewal if market starts offering carve-backs.
discoveryQuestions: If another public-health emergency landed in the middle of an election cycle, would Run-Test's facility/mail-handling protocols be defensible without insurance backstop?
Have any clients asked questions about Run-Test's pandemic protocols in the last contract cycle?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Innocent Insured Carve-Back on Criminal Acts Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF Best Practices — innocent insured protection where individual misconduct is alleged.
findings.policy_quote: Amendment Criminal/Dishonest/Knowingly Wrongful Acts (VP 03 08 07 17, End. #12): 'Innocent insured carve-out for natural persons (other than Named Insured) who did not participate in, ratify, or acquiesce. Defense provided until adjudication.'
findings.gap_description: The criminal/dishonest acts exclusion is properly modified with an innocent-insured carve-back — natural-person Insureds who didn't participate in, ratify, or acquiesce in alleged misconduct retain coverage, and defense is provided until final adjudication. Important in an election-services environment where political actors may level fraud allegations against the company without distinguishing among individuals.
findings.plain_english: If somebody at Run-Test was accused of misconduct but a senior executive or director knew nothing about it, the policy still defends the innocent person and the company until a court actually finds them guilty. That's how the language should read.
findings.recommendation: No action. Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Pending and Prior Litigation Date
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate, with retro on or before contract effective date.
findings.policy_quote: Pending and Prior Litigation Exclusion with Date (VP 02 89 10 17, End. #18): 'P&P Litigation Date: 3/26/2017. Excludes Loss/Claim Expenses arising out of pending or prior Claims, suits, or litigation existing prior to 3/26/2017, or future Claims related/associated with such matters.'
findings.gap_description: The P&P litigation date is set at 3/26/2017 — coincident with the master retro. Any pre-2017 latent matter is barred, including future claims that 'relate to' those prior matters. For a 50+ year company, this is a meaningful prior-acts cap and the 'related claims' language is potentially aggressive.
findings.plain_english: The policy excludes anything that was already in litigation or known before March 2017 — and anything that 'relates to' those older matters. The 'relates to' language can be invoked aggressively by carriers to deny new claims that have any thread of connection to old matters.
findings.recommendation: Maintain awareness of any pre-2017 litigation files; ensure they are documented and isolated from current operations to avoid 'related claims' arguments. At renewal, consider whether broader prior-acts language can be negotiated (often tied to a clean disclosure rep on the application).
discoveryQuestions: Were there any pre-2017 county disputes, demand letters, or claims-in-the-making that you'd want to make sure didn't get pulled forward into a 'related claims' argument?
Has your prior carrier or current carrier ever invoked a 'related claims' theory to consolidate or deny coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Disciplinary Proceeding Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — defense sublimits for regulatory/disciplinary actions.
findings.policy_quote: Amended §II.A Disciplinary Proceedings (VP 08 39 05 17, End. #15): 'Disciplinary Proceeding sublimit: $25,000 each / $50,000 aggregate. Deductible does not apply; does not erode Each Claim/Aggregate limits. No duty to appoint counsel.'
findings.gap_description: The Disciplinary Proceeding coverage is sublimited at $25K per proceeding / $50K aggregate, with no carrier duty to appoint counsel. For an election-services firm potentially facing state Secretary of State inquiries, FEC matters, or county audit reviews, $25K of defense will be exhausted quickly by a single competent regulatory defense matter.
findings.plain_english: If a state election authority opens a regulatory inquiry into Run-Test's operations, the policy gives you $25,000 toward defense — that's roughly 60-80 hours of senior outside-counsel time. A serious state inquiry will burn through that in a month.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher sublimit at renewal ($100K-$250K is achievable in this market for a clean-loss-history election firm) and ensure carrier accepts duty to defend rather than pay-as-incurred. If carrier holds line, document the gap and ensure D&O / Mgmt Liability or Cyber regulatory-defense coverage is robust.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Possibly partial — Cyber regulatory defense may apply for cyber-related inquiries; Mgmt Liability may apply for entity regulatory actions. Verify across program.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever been the subject of a state Secretary of State inquiry, county audit, or other regulatory review of your election operations?
Do you know what your own attorneys would charge for an aggressive multi-state regulatory inquiry — and how that compares to $25,000?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Subpoena Response Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — coverage adequacy for ancillary defense costs.
findings.policy_quote: Subpoena response sublimit: $2,500 per subpoena / $5,000 aggregate (per Dec page Item 4 limits structure).
findings.gap_description: Subpoena response sublimit is materially low ($2,500/$5,000) for a vendor handling 90M+ voter records and frequently subject to election-related discovery in voting-rights, recount, and political litigation involving its county clients.
findings.plain_english: When you get subpoenaed for documents (which is routine for an election vendor), the policy gives you $2,500 per subpoena to pay for legal review and production. That covers maybe a couple of hours of attorney time per subpoena.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher subpoena sublimit at renewal — $25K+ per subpoena is reasonable given operational subpoena frequency in election work.
discoveryQuestions: How often does Run-Test get served with subpoenas — for political litigation, recount disputes, voting-rights challenges, or even FOIA-adjacent requests?
How much does it typically cost to respond to a subpoena once your counsel reviews and produces records?

findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. The County Risk Manager may waive or alter this requirement, or accept self-insurance in lieu of any required policy of insurance...

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — TCPA / Unsolicited Communications Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: TCPA exclusion (VP 00 06 10 17 §IV.K): 'Excludes claims based on unsolicited faxes and electronic mail.'
findings.gap_description: Standard TCPA exclusion. Run-Test's outbound mail processing for counties is largely transactional and consent-based (voter registration, ballot delivery), but voter outreach mailings, sample ballot pushes, or election notification campaigns could be alleged to fall within TCPA-style consumer protection statutes if a recipient claims lack of consent.
findings.plain_english: TCPA-type lawsuits over unsolicited communications are excluded. Most ballot mail isn't consumer marketing, but if Run-Test ever takes on voter-outreach or election-notification mailings that fall on the wrong side of consent rules, those claims aren't covered.
findings.recommendation: Confirm operationally that Run-Test's mail products are election-mandated communications (ballots, official notices) rather than discretionary outreach. If discretionary outreach is offered, consider standalone media liability or CGL Personal & Advertising Injury coverage adequacy.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Potentially CGL Personal & Advertising Injury (need GL policy review — not provided in this audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test handle any voter outreach mailings beyond official ballots and election notices — newsletters, get-out-the-vote campaigns, candidate information?
