findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Tower Construction & Limits
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Convex Insurance UK Limited XPL000040-0425: $5,000,000 policy limit / $5,000,000 attachment point. Follow form excess to Gemini VIPL056495 primary Tech E&O. Total Tech E&O tower: $10,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Properly structured $5M xs $5M follow-form excess Tech E&O placement creating a $10M total tower. Convex is a dedicated Excess Professional Liability carrier (not a commercial umbrella), which is the correct vehicle to stack on E&O — Sacramento §II.E only prohibits umbrella stacking on PL, not dedicated excess PL.
findings.plain_english: The excess E&O is properly built — $5M sitting over the $5M primary creates a $10M tower for Tech E&O. The structure is appropriate: it's a dedicated Excess E&O policy, not a general umbrella, so the contractual limitation on stacking umbrellas onto E&O doesn't apply.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify excess attachment point continues to match primary limit (no inadvertent gap if primary limit changes).

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Conditional Follow-Form 'More Restrictive' Clause
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements...
findings.policy_quote: Section I (XPL-300): 'If any Underlying Policy includes any more restrictive coverage, terms, definitions, exclusions, conditions, or limitations, then this policy will follow the more restrictive provisions of any Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Conditional (not pure) follow form. Every restrictive provision on the Gemini primary — split limits, Client Print Media exclusion, Delay exclusion, Hardware/Electrical concurrent-cause language, mail-processing later retro — flows up to and binds the Convex excess. The excess does NOT cure any primary gap; it only amplifies the primary's limits within the primary's scope.
findings.plain_english: The excess policy is only as good as the primary. Every gap in the Gemini primary (the split limits, the Client Print Media exclusion, the Delay exclusion) flows straight up to the Convex excess. Fixing the primary fixes the tower; not fixing the primary leaves a $10M policy with $1M of effective coverage on certain claim types.
findings.recommendation: Treat all primary E&O fixes as urgent — they automatically improve the entire $10M tower. Inversely, any restrictive endorsement added to Gemini at renewal will worsen Convex too, so audit primary endorsements at every renewal cycle.
discoveryQuestions: Do you and your prior broker treat the primary E&O renewal as the more important negotiation, knowing every restriction added there flows up to your $10M total tower?
When the underwriter offers a small premium credit in exchange for a new exclusion on the primary, has anyone walked you through the impact on the excess too?

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Sublimits Not Extended
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — sublimit treatment in excess layers.
findings.policy_quote: Section II (XPL-300): 'If any Underlying Policy grants coverage subject to a sublimit of liability, this policy shall not afford such coverage, however this policy shall recognize any reduction or exhaustion of the Attachment Point by payments with respect to such coverage pursuant to that Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Any sublimited Gemini coverage (Disciplinary Proceeding $25K/$50K, Subpoena $2.5K/$5K, Supplementary Payments $5K/claim) is NOT extended at the excess layer — but those sublimit payments DO erode the $5M attachment point. Net effect: the insured pays for sublimited coverage with no excess support, but the dollars still consume the path to the excess.
findings.plain_english: If your primary policy has a $25,000 sublimit on a regulatory inquiry, the excess won't add another $25,000 — it just won't respond to that coverage at all. But those $25K of payments DO eat into the $5M you need to use up before excess kicks in. So sublimits on the primary become a one-way street.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher sublimits on Gemini primary (see disciplinary proceeding finding). Accept that the excess won't ever supplement sublimits — fix sublimits at the primary level.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Retroactive Date Match
findings.contract_quote: Retro Date must be on or before the date of the Agreement... (Sacramento §V.A); retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract... (Maricopa §8.2.3)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Retroactive Date Endorsement (XPL-502): 'Retroactive Date: 03/27/2017 — matches the underlying Gemini retro date. No retro gap.'
findings.gap_description: Convex retro 03/27/2017 matches the Gemini primary retro precisely. No retro gap at the excess layer. (Subject to the same split-limits caveat as the primary — see finding-002.)
findings.plain_english: The excess and primary share the same prior-acts reach-back date — no daylight between them. Solid construction.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Maintenance of Underlying (Favorable Construction)
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella §6 — Maintenance of underlying insurance.
findings.policy_quote: Section IV.D (XPL-300): If insured fails to maintain underlying or renews/replaces with lesser coverage, Convex is liable only as if the underlying had been fully maintained. Failure to maintain does NOT void the policy but the excess attaches as if the underlying limit were intact (insured eats the gap).
findings.gap_description: This is the favorable of the two common maintenance constructions. The excess is NOT voided for failure to maintain — it simply attaches as if the underlying were fully maintained. Insured assumes the gap dollars but retains the excess capacity above attachment. Compare to the more punitive 'failure-to-maintain-voids-policy' construction common in some commercial umbrellas.
findings.plain_english: If for any reason the primary policy's limits get impaired or replaced with weaker coverage, the excess doesn't disappear — it just acts like the primary was still full strength, and Run-Test eats the gap dollars. That's the better of the two ways this clause can be written.
findings.recommendation: No action — maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Right and Duty to Defend on Drop-Down
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella §11 — Right and Duty to defend when underlying limits exhausted.
findings.policy_quote: Section IV.B.2 (XPL-300): 'We will have the right and duty to defend any claim made or suit brought or proceeding instituted against an Insured to which this policy applies if the applicable limits of Underlying Policies have been exhausted.'
findings.policy_page: Not extracted — referenced from analysis JSON
findings.gap_description: Convex grants right AND duty to defend once Gemini exhausts. This is best-in-class for follow-form excess and uncommon in pure-follow-form constructions.
findings.plain_english: Once the primary policy's $5M is paid out, Convex doesn't just write checks — it picks up active defense duty too. That's a strong consumer-friendly provision.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Underlying Policy Number Discrepancy
findings.contract_quote: Verification of Coverage / COI & Endorsements: 'CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below.'
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Dec page Item 5 references Gemini policy VIPL056495; Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301, page 13) shows VIPL055885.
findings.gap_description: Administrative discrepancy — both numbers are Gemini, but the Convex Dec and Schedule of Underlying don't agree on the underlying policy number. In a coverage dispute, a carrier could (in theory) argue the schedule controls and that Convex sits over a different underlying than the actual primary. Risk is low and curable but should be cleaned up.
findings.plain_english: The excess policy's paperwork has two different numbers for your primary E&O — one on the Dec page, one on the schedule. It's almost certainly a clerical error since both numbers are with Gemini, but get it corrected so a carrier can't argue paperwork ambiguity if a big claim ever arises.
findings.recommendation: Issue endorsement request to Convex to correct the underlying policy number to match the in-force Gemini policy (VIPL056495 per current Dec). Should be a no-cost MCO (manuscript change order) endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Named Insured Entity Mismatch (LLC vs Inc)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §3 — Named Insureds list for each policy and flag any missing.
findings.policy_quote: Convex Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC' (LLC). Gemini primary Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, Inc.' (Inc).
findings.policy_file: RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf / Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: The primary E&O lists 'Runbeck Election Services, Inc.' while the Convex excess lists 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC.' Convex's Insured definition follows form to the underlying — so if the underlying Insured is 'Inc' but the named Convex insured is 'LLC,' there's at minimum a paperwork mismatch. The Cyber policy was corrected via Policy Change #1 effective 4/1/2025 to reflect 'LLC' — suggesting the LLC is the operative legal entity. The primary E&O appears to be the outlier still showing 'Inc.'
findings.plain_english: The legal entity name on your primary E&O says 'Inc.' but the excess and Cyber say 'LLC.' If you've reorganized as an LLC, the primary E&O paperwork is wrong — and that mismatch can be exploited at claim time to argue the wrong entity is insured.
findings.recommendation: Issue endorsement on the Gemini primary to correct Named Insured to match the operative legal entity (LLC, per Cyber correction). This is a no-cost name-change endorsement (typically IL 12 01 11 85 or carrier equivalent). Verify across CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, and Umbrella as well — the Cyber cross-reference notes those policies still show 'Inc' too.
discoveryQuestions: What is the operative legal entity for Run-Test today — Runbeck Election Services, Inc. or LLC?
When was the most recent corporate restructuring, and was every insurance policy updated to match?
Are there any subsidiary or affiliate entities that should also be listed (Runbeck Properties, Runbeck Investments, Runbeck Graphics) on every policy in the program?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — $5M Limit Compliance vs Maricopa Minimum
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000. Defense costs are part of and not in addition to the Aggregate Limit. Aggregate is shared across all 14 coverage lines.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $5M PER OCCURRENCE Cyber. AmTrust policy provides $4M AGGREGATE (not per-occurrence), shared across 14 coverage lines, with defense costs eroding limits. Two separate gaps: (1) $1M+ shortfall on stated limits ($4M < $5M); (2) per-occurrence vs aggregate structure mismatch — aggregate erodes across the year. Effective indemnity capacity on a single significant claim is roughly $800K-$1.6M after defense erosion. This is an uncured contract breach as of policy inception 4/1/2025.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires $5M of Cyber. You have $4M, and that $4M is shared across every type of cyber claim and burns down with defense costs. On a single major breach, after lawyers and forensics get paid, your effective coverage is closer to $1M-$1.5M — a fraction of what Maricopa contracted for. You are out of contractual compliance from day one of this policy term.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — increase Cyber tower to at least $5M with structure that satisfies 'per occurrence' language. Options: (1) endorse AmTrust to $5M aggregate (likely additional $5K-$15K premium); (2) add $5M xs $4M excess Cyber layer (cleaner contract compliance and per-occurrence interpretation); (3) replace AmTrust with $5M-limit market (Beazley, AIG, Coalition, At-Bay, etc. routinely write $5M for election-services scale). Recommend Option 2 or 3. Also notify Maricopa Risk Management of cure timeline to mitigate material-breach exposure under §8.2.2 / §8.2.15.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No Cyber excess in program. Hanover Umbrella (per cross-reference) does NOT follow form to Cyber.
discoveryQuestions: Were you aware that Maricopa requires $5M of Cyber and your current policy provides $4M aggregate with defense inside the limits?
Has your prior broker walked you through what 'shared aggregate across 14 coverage lines' actually means for your claim recovery?

If a major county data event happened in October before the November election, how would you fund the gap between the $4M policy and the actual cost of forensics, breach counsel, regulatory defense, business interruption, and notification at scale?
Has anyone from Maricopa Risk Management ever asked to see the full Cyber policy or just accepted the COI?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Defense Within Limits + Shared Aggregate (Effective Capacity Erosion)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for... defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: Defense Within Limits PLUS shared aggregate across 14 coverage lines means a typical cyber event consumes 60-80% of the $4M aggregate on forensics, breach counsel, PR, and regulatory defense before any indemnity is paid. Effective indemnity recovery on a single moderate-to-large event is approximately $800K-$1.6M against a $4M nominal policy. For a vendor handling 90M voter records, this is materially inadequate.
findings.plain_english: Every dollar your lawyers and forensic firm bill on a cyber claim comes out of your $4M policy — and on a real cyber event, the lawyers and forensic firm will eat the majority of that $4M before the first dollar of breach response, regulatory fine, or business interruption indemnity is paid. So your $4M is functionally more like $1M-$1.5M of usable indemnity.
findings.recommendation: Restructure cyber tower with (1) defense-outside-limits or (2) substantially higher limit with stable aggregate, OR (3) layered tower so erosion on the primary doesn't gut total capacity. Coalition, Beazley, AIG and At-Bay routinely offer DOL on $5M+ programs at this revenue band.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone explain to you that legal fees and forensics on a major cyber claim could consume 60-80% of your $4M before you see a dollar of breach response money?
If a county sued you, regulators investigated, you needed forensics, AND business operations were interrupted — all from one cyber incident — would $4M cover all of that?
Has your IT or security team estimated what a credible breach scenario would cost end-to-end?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Cyber Deception / Social Engineering Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance... shall include... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception/Social Engineering: Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000.
findings.gap_description: Sublimit equals retention — effective recoverable on any single loss ≤ $250K is $0. On a $300K loss, recovery = $50K. On a $500K loss, recovery = $250K (50% of loss). Maricopa §8.2.13 explicitly requires 'computer fraud coverage' and 'funds transfer loss' which is functionally social engineering / impersonation fraud — the most common large-dollar cyber claim type for vendors managing county AP/AR flows. This is phantom coverage and an uncured contract breach.
findings.plain_english: Social engineering coverage is structured so the retention equals the limit — meaning if a fraudster impersonates a county and tricks your AP team into wiring $200K, you'd recover ZERO. On a $500K loss you'd recover $250K. This is the most common big-dollar cyber claim hitting vendors today, and your coverage on it is essentially worthless.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — increase Cyber Deception limit to at least $1M with retention of $25K-$50K (separate from the $50K policy retention). This is a low-cost endorsement on most cyber forms ($2K-$8K premium typical). Also implement operational controls: callback verification on wire instructions over $25K, dual approval on payment changes, vendor-onboarding identity verification.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Crime/Fidelity policy may cover — verify if Run-Test maintains a separate Crime policy (not in audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: How often does your AP team process wire transfers or change-of-banking-instructions requests on behalf of county clients or vendors?
If a fraudster spoofed a county elections director's email and instructed your AP team to redirect a $200,000 payment, how would your team detect it?
Did you know that on any single loss up to $250,000, your current cyber policy pays you ZERO under the Cyber Deception coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Continuity / Retroactive Date Gap (50+ Year Operating History)
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract...
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: 04/01/2023.
findings.gap_description: Continuity Date is 4/1/2023, only 2 years before current inception. Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history with continuous handling of voter data. Persistent threat actors who gained unauthorized access prior to 4/1/2023 — a known threat in the elections sector — would not trigger coverage. Need to confirm against each county contract effective date that the continuity date predates each contract.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy only reaches back to April 2023. If a hacker has been quietly inside your systems since 2021 and discovers themselves (or is discovered) tomorrow, the policy may say the breach started before its retro and refuse to respond. For a company your size and tenure, the retro should reach back further.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate retro extension at renewal — 5-7 years is achievable for a clean-claim-history election-services firm. If incumbent carrier won't extend, replace at renewal; most major cyber markets will offer 'full prior acts' or 5+ year retros for this risk profile. Confirm continuity date predates each active county contract effective date.
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test been the subject of any prior cyber events — even small ones — that pre-date April 2023?
Does your IT security team monitor for advanced persistent threats that may have established access months or years ago?
When did each of your active county contracts begin? Are any of them effective before April 2023?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Additional Insured Status for Maricopa County
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds.
findings.policy_quote: No Additional Insured endorsement visible on Cyber policy. Endorsement schedule (Item 8) blank in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.7 expressly requires AI status on all policies except WC and E&O. Cyber is NOT carved out and therefore must include AI status. No AI endorsement is visible on the AmTrust Cyber. Many cyber forms do not accommodate AI status; if AmTrust will not endorse, Run-Test is in uncured contract breach and may need to replace cyber to satisfy Maricopa.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires the County to be named as an Additional Insured on your Cyber policy. The current policy doesn't appear to do that, and many cyber forms can't be endorsed for AI. You're out of contractual compliance, and curing it may require replacing the cyber carrier.
findings.recommendation: Request AI endorsement from AmTrust immediately for Maricopa County. If AmTrust declines (common in cyber), notify client and (a) shop replacement cyber market that will endorse AI status, OR (b) negotiate written waiver from Maricopa Risk Management acknowledging cyber-form limitations. Don't ignore — Maricopa §8.2.2 makes lapse a material breach.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone tell you Maricopa requires the County to be named as an Additional Insured on your Cyber policy specifically?
If AmTrust won't endorse the County as AI on Cyber, are you willing to switch carriers, or would you prefer we negotiate a waiver from Maricopa?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Waiver of Subrogation for Maricopa
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: No Waiver of Subrogation endorsement visible on Cyber policy.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.8 requires WoS on all policies except WC and E&O. Cyber is NOT carved out. No WoS endorsement visible on AmTrust Cyber. Uncured contract breach.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your Cyber carrier to waive its right to come after the County for reimbursement after paying a claim. The policy doesn't show that endorsement. If a cyber event involved any County system or action, AmTrust could subrogate against the County — exactly what the contract prohibits.
findings.recommendation: Request WoS endorsement from AmTrust. Most cyber forms accommodate this. If declined, treat as part of the larger replacement conversation alongside the AI gap and the $5M shortfall.
discoveryQuestions: Has your Cyber carrier confirmed in writing that it has waived subrogation rights against Maricopa County?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Primary & Noncontributory for Maricopa
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: No Primary & Noncontributory endorsement visible on Cyber policy.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.4 program-level P&NC requirement applies to all required policies including Cyber. No endorsement visible.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your insurance to pay first before any County coverage gets touched. The Cyber policy doesn't have that endorsement. Lower-priority gap than AI/WoS but still a contract breach.
findings.recommendation: Request P&NC endorsement on Cyber from AmTrust at next opportunity (often automatic on AI endorsement; verify language).
discoveryQuestions: Does your Cyber COI to Maricopa indicate primary and noncontributory status?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Designated Entity 30-Day Cancellation Notice
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: No Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement visible. Endorsement schedule blank in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 requires direct 30-day cancellation/material-change notice to the County, not the standard ACORD COI disclaimer. Cyber forms don't always include this; need to confirm or endorse. Note: Sacramento §VI.A.2 places notification obligation on the Contractor (not the carrier), so a Designated Entity NOC isn't required there — but Maricopa is more demanding.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your Cyber carrier to give the County 30 days' written notice if anything material changes on the policy or the policy gets cancelled. The standard ACORD COI 'endeavor to notify' language doesn't satisfy this — you need an actual endorsement. If it's not on the policy, you're in breach of §8.2.15.
findings.recommendation: Request Designated Entity NOC endorsement on Cyber for Maricopa County (and any other counties with similar requirements). Verify across all required policies in the program (CGL, Auto, WC, Umbrella, Mgmt Liability — all currently listed in cross-reference but not in this audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: Has the carrier provided a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement naming Maricopa County?
If the Cyber policy were cancelled mid-term, would Maricopa get 30 days' written notice directly from the carrier?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Proof of Loss Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include... defense, and claims expenses...
findings.policy_quote: Proof of Loss sublimit: $250,000 / Retention $50,000.
findings.gap_description: Proof of Loss sublimit caps forensic accounting expense at $200K (after $50K retention). For a multi-million-dollar BI claim documentation, $200K of forensic accounting may be inadequate, particularly given that the policy's $4M shared aggregate makes BI claim proof-up the most likely scenario where forensic accounting is needed.
findings.plain_english: Proving up a business-interruption loss requires a forensic accountant and that work is sublimited to $200K. On a serious BI claim that work alone can run $300K-$500K. You'd be funding the gap.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher Proof of Loss sublimit at renewal — $500K is achievable in most market.
discoveryQuestions: If you had to prove a $3M business-interruption loss to the carrier, how much would your CFO need in forensic-accounting fees to do that?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Choice of Law (NY for AZ Insured)
findings.contract_quote: Compliance with insurance requirements... and applicable state law.
findings.policy_quote: Choice of Law: New York.
findings.gap_description: Insured is Arizona-domiciled with operations in 31+ states. NY choice-of-law clause affects litigation venue, recoverable damages categories, punitive damage availability, and statute-of-limitations interpretation in any coverage dispute. Not a coverage gap per se but a structural item to flag.
findings.plain_english: If you ever fight your cyber carrier over coverage, the dispute will be decided under New York law, not Arizona's. Different states interpret policy language differently — NY is generally insurer-friendly on choice-of-law issues. Worth knowing, not necessarily worth changing.
findings.recommendation: No immediate action. Review at renewal whether replacement market offers AZ choice-of-law (some carriers will). Ensure outside counsel familiar with NY coverage law is identified for any future cyber dispute.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Surplus Lines Carrier (Informational)
findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII... (Sacramento §VI.A.1) ... AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++ (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Associated Industries Insurance Company (AmTrust) — placed via ANV Global Services Inc., surplus lines / non-admitted in Arizona. AM Best A- (Excellent) per cross-reference.
findings.gap_description: Cyber is a market routinely placed in the surplus lines channel. AmTrust/Associated Industries is rated A- (Excellent) — satisfies both Sacramento A-VII and Maricopa B++ minimums. AZ guaranty fund does not protect against insolvency of non-admitted carriers; informational only per audit methodology rule 15.
findings.plain_english: Cyber is normally placed with surplus lines carriers — it's not a defect. The carrier rating (A-) meets both county requirements. The only consideration is no AZ guaranty fund backstop in an insolvency, which is the same trade-off as any surplus lines placement.
findings.recommendation: Document current AM Best rating of Associated Industries Insurance Company in client file. Re-verify at each renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Regulatory Fines & Penalties Coverage
findings.contract_quote: [Cyber] policy shall include... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: Regulatory Fines and Penalties sublimit $4,000,000 / Retention $50,000 (per Dec page sublimits).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires the Cyber policy to cover both regulatory DEFENSE COSTS and FINES AND PENALTIES (where insurable by law). The Dec page shows $4M sublimit on Regulatory Fines and Penalties, but the underlying form language defining what fines/penalties are actually insurable is not visible in the extracted excerpt. Many cyber forms exclude or sublimit fines that are uninsurable as a matter of public policy in certain states.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires fines and penalties — not just defense costs — to be covered. The dec shows a $4M sublimit, but we need to read the form language to see whether the carrier actually pays fines or only defends against them. This is a gating question before declaring contract compliance on this point.
findings.recommendation: Pull full Cyber policy form (not just dec page excerpt). Read the regulatory coverage grant and any state-by-state insurability carve-outs. Confirm that AZ and CA fines/penalties — to the extent insurable as a matter of public policy — are paid, not just defended.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Named Insured Entity Correction (Cross-Program Comparison)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §3 — Named Insureds list for each policy and flag any missing.
findings.policy_quote: Insured Name Change (IL 12 01 11 85, Policy Change #1) effective 4/1/2025: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC; Runbeck Properties, LLC; Runbeck Investments LLC; Runbeck Graphics Inc.'
findings.gap_description: Cyber is the ONLY policy in the program where the LLC entity-type correction has been processed (per cross-reference notes). Cyber lists Runbeck Election Services LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, and Runbeck Graphics Inc as Policyholders. Worth highlighting that the cyber broker/carrier handled this correctly so the rest of the program can be brought into alignment.
findings.plain_english: The Cyber policy is the only one with the entity-name correction done right — and it covers all four Runbeck legal entities. Use this as the template for cleaning up the rest of the program.
findings.recommendation: Use Cyber Named Insured schedule as the template; replicate across all program policies (E&O, CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, Umbrella).

findings.requirement_type: Program — General Liability Policy Not Provided for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. (Maricopa §8.2.10) ... Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000... Each Occurrence: $1,000,000 (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Cross-reference to Hanover CGL policy noted in Cyber analysis but Hanover CGL not provided in this audit batch.

The Hanover CGL policy (referenced in Cyber cross-references) is not provided for analysis. RMF CGL checklist (33 items including Additional Insured, Per Project Aggregate, Mental Anguish, Care/Custody/Control, Fellow Employee, Notice & Knowledge, Damage to Premises, Pollution, Faulty Work, Hired/Non-Owned, etc.) cannot be evaluated without the policy.

Both Sacramento ($1M/$2M) and Maricopa ($2M/$4M/$4M) have specific GL requirements with Additional Insured, Waiver of Subrogation, Primary/Noncontributory, blanket contractual, and XCU coverage requirements. findings.requirement_type: Program — Commercial Auto Policy Not Provided for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles. (Maricopa §8.2.11) ... Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. (Sacramento §III.B)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Cross-reference to Hanover Auto policy noted but not provided in audit batch.
findings.gap_description: Auto policy not provided for analysis. RMF Commercial Auto checklist (18 items including Additional Insured, Symbols 1/2 vs 7, Hired/Non-Owned, Drive Other Car, Mobile Equipment, Fellow Employee, UM/UIM, Notice & Knowledge, Lease Gap) cannot be evaluated.

Maricopa requires $2M CSL — and importantly, Auto §8.2.11 doesn't inline-mention umbrella attachment, creating an interpretive ambiguity if the underlying Auto is at $1M with $10M umbrella stacking on top. We need the Hanover Auto to verify.

findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR, that arise out of or are in any way connected with CONTRACTOR's performance under this Agreement and that in any way, directly or indirectly, contingently or otherwise, affect or might reasonably affect COUNTY, CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's signature-verification process for mail ballots involve any storage or processing of signature data?
Are you offering any biometric authentication services (fingerprint, voiceprint) to counties?
Have you operated in Illinois, Texas, or Washington — states with active biometric privacy statutes?

findings.requirement_type: General Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program

findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.10 Pg 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.A Pg 2 of 4
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy was provided in this program audit submission. The only policies received were Hanover Workers' Compensation (WD4-H218283-06) and Hartford Twin City Management Liability (59 KB 0575120-24).

findings.plain_english: Run-Test does not appear to have a General Liability policy on file with us. CGL is the foundation policy of any commercial insurance program — it covers premises slip-and-falls, bodily injury to third parties, products liability, and operations claims. A bodily injury or property damage claim from any county, vendor, voter, or visitor would have no coverage. Both your Sacramento and Maricopa contracts require this. Without it, every county contract you have is in technical breach and every claim is paid out of operating cash. This is the highest-priority item in the entire audit.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a GL policy exists and was simply not provided for review. If none exists, place a CGL immediately at $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate / $4M products-completed minimum (to satisfy Maricopa's higher tier). Ensure ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form, blanket contractual, blanket AI (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37), Primary & Noncontributory (CG 20 01), Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04), Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03 if any construction is performed), no XCU exclusion, and Notice/Knowledge endorsement limited to officer/risk manager.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through the last time a member of the public — a voter, a visitor, a vendor — was injured at one of your facilities. Where did the bill go, and what would happen if it occurred today?

Your Sacramento contract requires a $1M/$2M GL with no added exclusions, and Maricopa requires $2M/$4M with explicit no-XCU language — when was the last time someone walked through every endorsement on your GL to make sure neither of those conditions is breached?
If a county sued you tomorrow because a defective ballot envelope caused mail delivery problems statewide, do you know which policy responds to the products liability claim — and at what limit?

(Maricopa §8.2.11). Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. (Sacramento §III.B)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.11 Pg 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.B Pg 2 of 4
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided in this program audit submission.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports ballots, election technology, and printing materials to county sites across 31 states. Without an Auto policy: any vehicle accident causing third-party injury or property damage during election logistics is uninsured beyond personal coverage that almost certainly excludes business use. findings.plain_english: We don't have an Auto policy on file. Election services means you're moving ballots, mail, and equipment to courthouses and post offices constantly — by truck, by employee car, by hired carrier. If an employee on a courthouse run rear-ends a school bus, your operating cash pays for it. If you don't own vehicles but rent them, you still need Hired Auto coverage. If employees use their own cars for ballot pickup, you still need Non-Owned Auto Liability. Personal auto policies categorically exclude business use; the carrier denies and the exposure lands on the company. Maricopa requires $2M CSL — there is currently $0.
findings.recommendation: Confirm a Commercial Auto policy exists. If none, place Auto immediately at $2M CSL on a Symbol 1 (Any Auto) basis — covering owned, hired, and non-owned. discoveryQuestions: How does a tray of ballots actually move from your facility to a county elections office — your trucks, hired carriers, employees in personal cars, or all three?
If an employee rear-ended someone tomorrow on the way to a county dropoff, whose insurance pays — yours, theirs, or both — and have you ever tested that?

Maricopa requires $2M CSL. Sacramento requires $1M. If we don't have an Auto policy, every certificate you've issued under those contracts is technically unsupported — when was the last time anyone reviewed the COIs for accuracy?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions — Policy Entirely Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. (Sacramento §II.D, §III.E) ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement ... CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. (§V.A–C)
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Professional Liability or Errors & Omissions policy was provided. Sacramento's contract expressly bars umbrella from satisfying this requirement: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable ... that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... (other than Professional Liability) ...' (Sacramento §II.E)
findings.gap_description: Run-Test renders election services — printing, mailing, processing, ballot handling, election mail sorting, emergency support technology — to local, county and state election officials across 31 states. This is textbook professional services exposure. The Hartford D&O policy expressly EXCLUDES claims arising from 'rendering or failure to render any services for fees' (Endorsement 19 — Manufacturing and Professional Service Exclusion, PP 00 H350 00 0616, Pg 85). Therefore the company has NO mechanism — neither standalone E&O nor entity-liability under D&O — to respond to a county claim alleging negligent ballot processing, miscount, mail handling failure, or election delivery error. Sacramento requires $1M/$1M PL on a claims-made or occurrence form with continuous retro coverage; umbrella expressly cannot fill this gap.
findings.plain_english: Election services IS professional services — and you have no policy that covers it. The Hartford D&O specifically excludes anything arising from 'rendering or failure to render services for fees,' which is your entire revenue line. If a county sues because ballots arrived late, were misprinted, or were processed incorrectly — and the suit alleges negligence in your election services — there is currently zero coverage anywhere in the program. Sacramento expressly prohibits using the umbrella to fix this gap. This is the single most existential coverage gap for your business model. A $1M E&O premium is small money compared to a county suing for damages from a botched primary.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone Election Services Professional Liability / Technology E&O immediately. Limits: minimum $1M/$1M to satisfy Sacramento; recommend $5M+ given operational scope (90M voters, 31 states). Definition of Professional Services MUST expressly include: ballot printing/design, election mail sorting and delivery, voter file processing, election technology services, ballot envelope manufacturing, signature verification support, and emergency election support. Retro date on or before the earliest active county contract. Confirm carrier offers full prior acts. Consider a combined E&O + Cyber form to also address Maricopa cyber requirement (see finding-004).
discoveryQuestions: When a county tells you ballots arrived late or were misprinted, what is your contractual exposure — and is anything in your insurance program designed to defend that allegation?

Your Hartford D&O has an exclusion that strips coverage for 'rendering or failure to render any services for fees.' That is literally what Run-Test does — has anyone walked you through what the practical effect of that exclusion is on a county dispute?
Sacramento County won't allow you to use your umbrella to satisfy the Professional Liability requirement. If a Sacramento auditor reviews your COIs tomorrow, what do we show them?
If a county election challenge alleges that your processing led to a miscount, do you know who pays the defense lawyers and who pays the settlement?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program ($5M Required by Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses ..., network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber policy was provided. The Hartford Crime Coverage Part has narrow related coverages: Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud $2M; Deception Fraud / Social Engineering $15,000 (extremely low); and explicitly excludes 'theft or disclosure of trade secrets, intellectual property, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. ... or Data (unless covered under IA 7)' per PP 00 H600 00 0616 §V(V), Pg 55. Computer Systems Restoration sublimit $25,000 only.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no Cyber policy. Hartford Crime sublimits Pg 8 (Crime Dec) and Pg 55 (exclusion).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test serves 31 states + DC, impacting 90M+ registered voters, with election technology solutions including ballot printing, mailing, processing, signature verification, and emergency support technology. This is a maximum-exposure cyber profile: large PII repositories (voter rolls), election integrity stakeholders (state AGs, DOJ, CISA), foreign-adversary threat actors, and ransomware risk. Maricopa requires $5M cyber with the broadest possible enumerated specs (regulatory FINES & PENALTIES, third-party fidelity, business interruption, cyber extortion, computer fraud, funds transfer, breach notification, credit monitoring). NO Cyber policy is in the program. The Hartford Crime form expressly excludes data/IP theft, providing only $25K computer systems restoration and $15K social engineering. Voter PII breach, ransomware on election eve, regulatory investigation by state AGs — all uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Of every coverage gap in this program, this is the one that should keep the CFO and the board up at night. Run-Test handles voter records for 90 million Americans across 31 states. Election infrastructure is on every nation-state cyber actor's target list. A ransomware attack 30 days before a primary — locking your printing systems and threatening to release voter PII — would trigger forensic costs, ransom decisions, business interruption, breach notification to 31 state AGs, regulatory defense, civil class actions, and county lawsuits for delayed mail. The current program has none of this. Hartford's Crime policy has $15,000 for social engineering and excludes data breaches. Maricopa is requiring $5M expressly. If Maricopa audits the COI today, you cannot deliver evidence of compliance — and given your industry, an auditor at the State of Arizona or any other county is going to ask. This is the immediate priority alongside Professional Liability.
findings.recommendation: Place a standalone Cyber/Tech E&O form at $5M minimum (recommend $10M given national exposure). Required coverages must include: first-party (BI/extortion/data restoration), third-party (privacy/network/regulatory defense including FINES & PENALTIES — many forms exclude or sublimit fines, get them in), social engineering at full limit (not sublimited), business interruption AND dependent business interruption, system failure trigger, bricking, voluntary parting, reputational harm, PCI assessments, election-specific endorsements where available. Retro date on or before earliest cyber-aware contract. Coordinate with E&O (finding-003) — combined Tech E&O + Cyber from a carrier specializing in election services / govtech (Coalition, At-Bay, Beazley InfoSec, Chubb Cyber Plus) is the most efficient path.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware actor encrypted your printing and processing systems three weeks before a primary, how would the company respond in the first 24 hours — and who pays for the response team?
You're holding voter PII for tens of millions of Americans across 31 state regulatory regimes. If even one state AG opened an investigation tomorrow, who defends it and who pays the fines?

Maricopa County requires a $5M cyber policy with regulatory FINES coverage, third-party fidelity, and cyber extortion as listed must-haves. Do we have a current certificate that satisfies that contract today?
Has anyone — internally or with us — modeled what a publicly disclosed Run-Test breach would do to your county relationships and renewal pipeline?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted ... (Sacramento §II.E). If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. (Maricopa §8.2.9)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E Pg 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.9 Pg 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella/Excess policy was provided in this program audit.
findings.gap_description: No Umbrella policy is present. Even if GL/Auto were placed at the $2M Maricopa underlying limits, a single bodily injury or product liability verdict in a federal/state court could exhaust primary GL aggregates within one claim. Election services, mail handling, and physical operations all carry catastrophic loss potential. Run-Test as a PE-backed company also faces enhanced regulatory and litigation exposure. The contractual indemnification obligations in Maricopa §8.1.3 are expressly NOT capped at insurance limits — uninsured tail liability falls on the balance sheet.
findings.plain_english: There's no umbrella in the program. Even when we place GL and Auto at the right limits, a single catastrophic event — a multi-vehicle delivery accident, a serious workplace injury, a product liability suit — can blow through a $2M GL aggregate in a single claim. The umbrella sits on top to absorb that. Maricopa's contract is also explicit that nothing in the insurance limits caps your indemnification obligation — meaning the County can come after Run-Test's balance sheet for any shortfall above policy limits. For a PE-backed company at this revenue scale, a $10M umbrella is table stakes; $25M is more appropriate given the geographic and operational footprint.
findings.recommendation: Place a follow-form Commercial Umbrella with minimum $10M limit (recommend $25M given 31-state operations, election scrutiny, and PE ownership). Confirm: (a) follow-form on AI, WoS, P&NC; (b) per-project / per-location aggregate follows form; (c) drop-down for exhausted underlying aggregates; (d) Defense costs OUTSIDE limits (standard market) — flag if E&S placement; (e) maintenance-of-underlying clause does NOT result in coverage forfeiture for inadvertent lapse; (f) Notice & Knowledge endorsement limited to officer/risk manager. Schedule of Underlying must list GL, Auto, EL (under WC), Foreign Voluntary if applicable. Note: Sacramento §II.E and Maricopa §8.2.9 BOTH bar Umbrella from being applied to satisfy the Professional Liability $1M minimum — Umbrella does NOT cure finding-003.
discoveryQuestions: If a delivery vehicle were involved in a multi-vehicle accident with serious injuries to multiple parties, do you know what your maximum exposure is — and what limit you'd want to defend yourself with?

Your contracts with both Sacramento and Maricopa say insurance limits do NOT cap your indemnification obligation — meaning anything above the policy comes out of the company. How comfortable is the board with that exposure today?
Have you ever had a claim or near-claim that approached or exceeded a primary GL aggregate? What did that conversation with leadership look like?

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Manufacturing and Professional Services Exclusion (Hartford)
findings.contract_quote: (D&O coverage is broadly required by lender covenants, board governance and PE sponsor expectations; not contractually required by Sacramento or Maricopa, but core balance-sheet protection.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #19 EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT: 'The Insurer shall not be liable for Loss on account of any Claim made against any Insured based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) the malfunction of any product or product failure due to any deficiency, inadequacy, defect, or dangerous condition in such product or in its design or manufacture; or (2) the rendering of or failure to render any services for a fee, including any services rendered by an Insured for a customer or client of any Insured.' Carve-backs: securities-holder civil proceedings without Insured solicitation; Derivative Action / Derivative Demand. (PP 00 H350 00 0616)
findings.policy_page: Pg 85 — Endorsement #19, Hartford Twin City Management Liability 59 KB 0575120-24
findings.gap_description: This exclusion is the most damaging endorsement in the entire program for Run-Test's business model. Run-Test's revenue is entirely 'services for a fee' — printing, mailing, processing, election technology — to county/state customers. The exclusion bars D&O Side B (corporate reimbursement) and Side C (entity liability) coverage for any Claim arising from these core operations. The carve-backs only preserve coverage for: (a) securities-holder civil suits brought without insider solicitation; and (b) derivative actions/demands. This means: (i) a county lawsuit naming directors/officers individually for service-delivery failures = excluded; (ii) state AG investigations of corporate conduct re: election services = excluded; (iii) regulatory actions arising from product/service failures = excluded. For a PE-backed election services manufacturer, this exclusion neuters the policy's most likely-to-trigger applications. Aligns with 2026-03-24 lesson learned re: Hartford Private Choice Premier.
findings.plain_english: This is the worst endorsement in the policy for your business specifically. Hartford has carved out coverage for any claim arising from rendering services for fees or product malfunction. Your entire revenue line — every dollar — is 'services for a fee' to counties. So if a county sues your directors and officers personally because ballots were processed incorrectly, the policy will deny. The only things that are still covered are very narrow: shareholder lawsuits, and derivative actions. Functionally you have D&O coverage for Wall Street-style claims and almost nothing for the Main Street claims that would actually hit a privately held election services company. The PE sponsor should be aware of this — they probably are not.
findings.recommendation: At renewal (4/1/2026 expiry), prioritize replacing or renegotiating this exclusion. Options in order of preference: (1) Move to a carrier that does not impose this exclusion on election technology / govtech firms (e.g., AIG, Travelers Bond, Berkshire's BHSI, Chubb, Beazley) — many will quote without it; (2) Negotiate a carve-back for non-securities claims by governmental/contractual customers; (3) At minimum negotiate carve-back for non-indemnifiable Side A coverage; (4) If Hartford remains the carrier, demand the exclusion be deleted in exchange for a premium increase. Until renewal, advise the board in writing that D&O Side B/C coverage for service-delivery claims is materially limited. PE sponsor counsel should be looped in.
discoveryQuestions: If a county attorney named your CEO and CFO personally in a lawsuit alleging that Run-Test's ballot processing caused election errors, what's your understanding of how the D&O policy would respond?
Has the PE sponsor — Lincoln Shields or Black Mountain — ever asked you to confirm what is and isn't covered under your D&O for service-delivery disputes?

When was the last time your D&O policy was marketed to multiple carriers? Hartford's policy has an exclusion that strips coverage for almost every claim type your business would actually face — that's worth shopping aggressively at renewal.
If the Department of Justice or a state AG opened an investigation into your election services tomorrow, do you understand what investigation costs would and wouldn't be covered?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — IP / Confidential Information / Data Exclusion (Voter PII)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance ... losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information) ... (Maricopa §8.2.13)
findings.policy_quote: Crime §V(V): excludes loss involving 'theft or disclosure of trade secrets, intellectual property, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. (unless covered under IA 8 Identity Recovery), or Data (unless covered under IA 7).' Identity Recovery (IA 8) is restricted to personal identities of named officers/directors/risk managers/in-house counsel — NOT the business itself. Computer Systems Restoration (IA 7) sublimit $25,000.
findings.policy_page: Pg 55 — PP 00 H600 00 0616 §V(V); Pg 8 — Crime Dec sublimits
findings.gap_description: Run-Test holds voter records affecting 90M+ registered voters across 31 states. The Crime policy explicitly excludes data, IP and confidential information theft. The only data-restoration coverage is Computer Systems Restoration at $25,000 — a fraction of the cost of even a contained ransomware response. There is no first-party data privacy coverage, no breach notification coverage, no regulatory defense coverage anywhere in the program. Combined with finding-004, voter PII breach has zero meaningful coverage in the current program.
findings.plain_english: The Hartford Crime piece is what some companies use as a stand-in for cyber when they don't have a real Cyber policy. For Run-Test that doesn't work — the Crime form expressly excludes any loss tied to data, IP, or confidential information. The $25,000 of computer systems restoration wouldn't cover a single day of a real ransomware response. So even setting the Cyber gap aside (finding-004), the Crime piece doesn't quietly fill it.
findings.recommendation: Treat as part of the Cyber placement priority (finding-004). Do not rely on Crime IA 7 or IA 8 for any data-related exposure. Once Cyber is placed, ensure no double-indemnification gap between Cyber and Crime — coordinate definitions of 'Money,' 'Securities,' 'Computer Fraud,' and 'Funds Transfer Fraud' across both forms.
discoveryQuestions: If a Run-Test laptop containing voter signature images was stolen out of an employee's car, what would actually happen — who responds, who pays for notification to the affected voters?
Have you ever quantified the cost of breach notification to voters across your 31 states? Each state has different timing rules and some require credit monitoring at the carrier's cost.
Your Crime policy will not cover data loss. Did anyone explain to you that the $25,000 'Computer Systems Restoration' line is not a substitute for cyber coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Deception Fraud (Social Engineering) Sublimit Materially Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: Cyber ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction ... (Maricopa §8.2.13)
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part Declarations (Pg 8): Deception Fraud (Social Engineering) $15,000 limit per occurrence. Other Crime IAs (Employee Theft, Forgery, Inside/Outside Premises, Computer Fraud, Funds Transfer Fraud) all $2,000,000.
findings.policy_page: Pg 8, Crime Coverage Part Declarations, Hartford 59 KB 0575120-24
findings.gap_description: Social engineering attacks (CEO impersonation wire-transfer fraud, vendor email compromise) are the dominant theft vector for any company processing payments for counties or paying vendors at scale. The $15,000 sublimit is dramatically below industry norm ($250K-$500K standard, $1M+ for high-exposure firms). For a company with $5M-$25M revenue and county-payment workflows, a single CEO-impersonation wire of $250,000-$750,000 is plausible — and the policy will pay only $15,000 of it.
findings.plain_english: Social engineering is the modern bank heist. Someone impersonates your CEO or a county finance officer, sends an urgent wire request, and your AP team approves it. The Hartford Crime policy will pay $15,000. A single average loss is in the hundreds of thousands. That's not insurance, that's a deductible.
findings.recommendation: At renewal (4/1/2026), increase Deception Fraud / Social Engineering sublimit to a minimum of $250,000 and ideally to the full $2M Crime limit if available. If Hartford caps it at $250K-$500K, place separate Cyber form (per finding-004) with Social Engineering limit of $1M+. Implement carrier-required dual-authentication and callback-verification controls to maintain coverage; many carriers now require these as conditions precedent.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current process when someone in finance receives a wire-transfer request that looks urgent and comes from the CEO or a senior county contact?
Have any of your AP staff ever received a phishing or impersonation email that looked legitimate? How was it caught?
If a $300,000 wire went out tomorrow on a forged executive request, would the company recover it through insurance? The current sublimit is $15,000.

findings.requirement_type: D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary — Prior Acts Exclusion (1-Year Cutoff)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance / PE sponsor expectation: full prior acts continuity to entity formation or PE acquisition date.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #28 — Prior Acts Exclusion: 'The Insurer shall not be liable for any Loss in connection with any Claim based upon, arising from, or in any way related to any Wrongful Act actually or allegedly committed in whole or in part prior to August 18, 2023; or any Interrelated Wrongful Acts thereto.' Applies to D&O, EPLI AND Fiduciary. (PP 00 H033 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: Policy effective 8/18/2024; prior acts cutoff 8/18/2023 — only 1 year of retroactive coverage on a Run-Test entity that is decades old. Any wrongful act, employment practice, fiduciary breach, or related claim arising from conduct before 8/18/2023 is uninsured under all three liability coverage parts. For a PE-backed company (per CLAUDE.md guidance to scrutinize prior acts on PE deals), this is a meaningful concern — typical PE-driven D&O placements feature continuous prior acts back to the LBO date or earlier.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O, EPL, and Fiduciary policies only cover conduct from August 2023 forward. Run-Test has been operating for 50+ years. If an employee filed an EPL suit today alleging harassment that occurred in 2022 — uncovered. If a former plan participant sues over a fiduciary decision made before the policy started — uncovered. For a PE-backed company, this is a known soft spot that PE sponsor counsel often demands be fixed at renewal or via separate run-off coverage.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, negotiate full prior acts (back to entity inception or at minimum the PE acquisition date). If carrier resists, consider purchasing tail / Side A DIC over the existing primary, or place a separate runoff policy for pre-8/18/2023 exposures. Discuss with PE sponsor representatives — they may have cross-portfolio carrier arrangements that include better prior acts.
discoveryQuestions: When the PE sponsors acquired Run-Test, was there a tail policy purchased for pre-acquisition wrongful acts? If not, what coverage protects pre-acquisition conduct today?
If a former employee sued for retaliation alleging conduct from 2022, what's your understanding of how the EPL responds?
Has the PE sponsor's General Counsel reviewed your prior acts coverage on D&O? Most PE shops require continuous prior acts.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Split Prior or Pending Date on Upper $1M Layer
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance / placement integrity)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #34 — Amended Declarations Split Prior or Pending Date: '04/02/2024 ... applies ONLY to the additional/increased $1,000,000 layer in excess of the first $1,000,000.' (PP 00 H105 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: First $1M D&O has older Prior or Pending date; upper $1M layer (in excess) has 4/2/2024 P&P date. Any matter pending or threatened between 8/18/2023 and 4/2/2024 is excluded from the upper $1M but covered under the first $1M — creating a 'donut' where catastrophic claims exceeding $1M find no excess support if rooted in matters pending during that window.
findings.plain_english: Your first $1M of D&O has one effective date for prior matters; the second $1M (which only kicks in when the first is exhausted) has a different, later effective date. So if a board-level dispute or lawsuit was simmering in late 2023 to early 2024 and breaks today and exceeds $1M, the upper layer denies — even though the first $1M would respond. Most placements don't do this; it's a renewal-time fix.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request the upper $1M layer's Prior or Pending date be aligned with the first $1M's date (or eliminated entirely). If the carrier refuses, consider replacing the upper $1M with a different excess carrier that will provide aligned P&P.
discoveryQuestions: Are you aware of any board, employment, or fiduciary matter that was unresolved between August 2023 and April 2024 — even informally?
If a $1.5M D&O claim broke today and was rooted in something pending in late 2023, do you understand how only half of it would be covered?

findings.requirement_type: WC Designated Entity NOC — Sacramento and Maricopa Counties Not Listed
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. (Maricopa §8.2.15)
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342 (09 11) Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): 30 days written notice to designated entities. Schedule lists: 'El Paso County Contracts & Procurement Division ... Coconino County ... Amazon.com Services LLC.' Sacramento County and Maricopa County are NOT listed.
